utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 6th of November, 2007, my greetings to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, especially Ms. Dahl and her assistant. Let me greet Mr. Seselj as well, without forgetting of course the registrar who is getting to assist us throughout the trial proceedings, the usher, and the interpreters who help us in our work. Today we have convened our Pre-Trial Conference pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Indeed, during the Pre-Trial Conference the Trial Chamber is going to set the number of hours and witnesses, but before we get there this is the first time the full Bench is present at the hearing. On my right-hand side I have Judge Harhoff and on my left-hand side Judge Lattanzi, and we are going to be the Trial Chamber seized of this case. I was the Pre-Trial Judge and as such, it is my duty to finalise the pre-trial proceedings by tackling a few pending questions before moving on to the main item which is to fix the number of hours as well as the number of witnesses. With regard to the remaining questions as the Pre-Trial Judge, I went last week to the Detention Unit where Mr. Seselj is detained in order to see by myself what the working conditions were for him since he's representing himself. And together with the registrar, the court deputy, and the Legal Officer, the Senior Legal Officer, I was able to go into his cell and realise that the Detention Unit administration had given him a cell next to his in which he has on shelves his documents including the binders handed over to him by the Prosecution and the binders had been received by the Trial Chamber. However, Mr. Seselj, I had the distinct impression that you did not have enough space. That was my impression upon visiting you. You have a lot of documents, and it might be good that the Detention Unit administration give you another room in which you can store documents that you don't use right then or documents that you have already viewed and are less important for you so that you have available to you just right next door to your cell the main documents. In this way, that is at least the way I feel about it but I would like to know what your opinion is, you would have more room in order to process and manage all these documents because I was able to see that you had to put documents on the floor, and the lack of space is quite obvious. If you so apply, I think that my fellow Judges will also support your application to the prison management so that you have another room and are able to work as best you can. So, Mr. Seselj, on this issue do you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I appreciate your attentiveness; however, had I been filing these materials the way the OTP had been sending them over the past several days, not even the entire floor in prison would have been sufficient. I was trying to save space to a maximum because I singled out all the documents that were in the English language and sent them back to the OTP. As for most of the documents in the Serbian language, I took them out of the binders, and I filed them according to the subjects involved so that it would all be handy. These piles of paper are due to the fact that they were taken out of binders. It's been a long time now that there hasn't been enough space for binders. In this situation I've been managing pretty well. I still have enough space, and for the time being these two adjoining cells are sufficient. If the Prosecution meets all their obligations, possibly I will need yet another cell for storage, but I am sure that the OTP is never going to meet all their obligations because the OTP, quite simply, has not disclosed documents to me at all according to Rule 68(i). They have not disclosed to me transcripts from other cases that have to do with witnesses who are supposed to appear in this case as well. They haven't supplied me with these materials on paper and in the Serbian language. They insist on disks and DVDs. They have to meet their obligation. They have to send me the transcripts because that is the only thing I can use in proceedings, not DVDs, however they refuse to meet that obligation of theirs. Probably if they do not do so to the very end, I will not really need the space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall come back to this later on, but if I am not mistaken, right now you are satisfied with this additional cell that was made available to you. And depending on the documents to come, as you just said, it might then be necessary for you to get an extra cell. Very well. I take due note of this request of yours, but of course I am bound to approve this when the need arises. Last time, Mr. Seselj, I told you that as the Pre-Trial Judge I was going to meet with the Registrar in order to speak about the issue of the translation of your book once again. On this core let me say this. During the meeting I had, I was told - and this had somehow escaped me - in your book that is over 1.000 pages long, the Cyrillic alphabet is a small font. So as a matter of fact, we're not talking about 1.000 pages, but more than 2.000 pages if you have the usual font used in this Tribunal. So that's if they wanted to translate the book, they would have to translate 2.000 pages. I was told very clearly that they are not at all able to translate 2.000 pages, the 2.000 pages of your book. I took note of what I was told, and as far as I was concerned at my level I tried and endeavoured, and I would like to seek your view on this, too. At the latest Status Conference I had said that if 1.000 pages -- in fact, 2.000 pages were to be translated, you would need to recruit a translator for over one year, and one translator who would do nothing but that, so that has a cost. And you then said that in Belgrade you could have translations done for less money. So you had this idea which you suggested, and it's worth looking into for a while. At your level for the time being, would it be possible to consider two possible options, the first being that you obtain a publishing contract with an Anglo-Saxon publisher and the book is then translated and you provide us with the English translation, the book in English, and the solution would be that. The second option which may be more practical in nature is this: Together with your associates, could you try to have a translation agency in Belgrade or somewhere else that would give you a quotation for the cost it would involve to have the book translated, so you would have a quote, you would send it to the Registry, and the Registry, as part of the facilities you are entitled to pursuant to the Statute, would pay for the cost based on this estimation you would be given. In this way your book could be translated. So you would be satisfied and the cost would be met by the Registry, and in the ensuing discussion you would have the book fully available to you. And I suppose that you would then seek to tender it into evidence. So these are practical solutions. I must say - but I've said this already - the Registry and the entire Registry staff are doing their level best, their level best in order to make sure that your rights arising from the Statute and from the Rules are complied with and are such that you can defend yourself the best you can. I did not feel any reticence on their part. It's only that when they said they were not able to have the book translated is because they come up against a real problem, a real logistical problem, but unfortunately so you are not the only one on trial, there are other cases, other documents to be translated. So these are two options open to you. In this respect could you tell us what your feeling is, knowing - and I remind you so that you have really all the factors in mind, you know that the Trial Chamber is going to issue some trial guide-lines shortly in which we are going to talk about the admissibility of evidence, and you may not know - but I'm sure you know because you've often displayed your full knowledge of our proceedings - the jurisprudence in most Trial Chambers when it comes to books is that excerpts and not entire books are admitted because a passage may be relevant and have probative value. So there's no point in having a whole book with hundreds, if not thousands, of pages admitted whilst only the Judges or yourself would only insist on a very specific part of a book, a chapter for instance. So keep this in mind, please. The admission of a book, especially because of translation problems, is of a limited scope and it is also controlled by the Trial Chamber because it is impossible to tender thousands of pages that are very costly to be translated, whilst you may just need five lines in the book or five lines may be relevant at all. So this is what I wanted to convey to you by way of information. Now, as to the practical solutions that could be found by the Registry, what is your view on this? Last time indeed you told me that this was a very important book to you for your defence, and I endorsed what you said by putting on record that by reading the index of the book, one could see chapters that are directly linked to the indictment, be it only the whole chapter on the Greater Serbia in your book. So of course there is a link, there is no doubt about it, but there may be other chapters in the book that may have less of a link at first sight. So this is what I wanted to say. My colleagues and I would like to know what you think of these possible solutions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm going to deal with two problems. The first problem is the problem of the significance of this book to my defence and the other one is the technical problem of translation itself. If you look at the nature of the indictment issued against me, you and your colleagues can see that I am being tried for atrocious war crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a problem with the translation into French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had it and then I lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please make sure that channel 5 is on, please. I can hear. Go ahead, Mr. Seselj, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that one has to look at the nature of the indictment issued against me. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. There still is a problem. Very well. Go ahead. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, I would like to deal with two basic problems that have to do with this book. The first one is of substantive significance, that is to say for my defence; and the second one is the problem of its translation. If you look at the nature of the indictment issued against me, you will see that I have been indicted of terrible war crimes that I allegedly committed through hate speech as I preached my nationalist ideology that I'm proud of. Then through the indictment and through the pre-trial brief, the OTP shows that they did not understand my ideology at all. This brings us to the question of whether you as the Trial Chamber will be in a position to understand it. My collected works to this day amount to 103 books. All my political speeches are included there, all my interviews for newspapers, texts about me, then my TV duels, my court proceedings because I have been tried about 20 times until now, and only on account of what I said not because of crime. Out of this enormous body of work, I singled out only two books, one I immediately proffered for interpretation, and that is "The Roman Catholic Criminal Project of the Croatian nation." The Prosecution cannot accuse me of having put down Croats if they do not understand what I'm talking about in terms of present-day Croats. I'm saying that the Roman Catholic church as a criminal organization projected this false Croatian nation, having stolen the name of a former medieval Slavic people, the Croats, who virtually went extinct in the time of the Turks. They now invented these new Croats and turned them against their ethnic mainstream. That is hard for people who come from the other parts of the world to understand, however, to understand the nature of the civil wars that were waged in the territory of the former Yugoslavia I believe it is indispensable to read that book. The second book is the ideology of Serbian nationalism. The Prosecution itself translated more than one-third of this book. You have that among the exhibits. The Prosecution understood the importance of this book. They don't understand the content of the book yet but they understand how important it is and they believe that they can use it to support their own thesis. Without this book, without those two books, my defence is virtually impossible and I was very modest on that score. In 2003, here in this courtroom, I handed over to the Prosecutor 80 of my books. They picked this up, they read them, they leafed through them, they got documents out of them, and they already built into exhibits many of these documents and interviews. Until now, they translated more material from my books than what the volume of these entire two books is. They translated more until now, they translated more than 2.000 pages from my books. I'm just giving you this for the sake of proportion so that you would see what kind of problem we're dealing with. Secondly, I base my defence on the need to use half of the proceedings or more than half for my own testimony, my own testimony will be based on these books and other things. That is the only way in which I was involved in these crimes that the Prosecutor has charged me with. I have no other involvement in crimes except for what I said and what I wrote. These are verbal deeds or the deed of writing, but nothing more than that. They have been trying to construct something, but that hasn't been very successful, you'll see that through the proceedings. Secondly, we come to the problem of translation. The Registry could have dealt with it already. They have their own office in Belgrade. I cannot do the work of the Registry -- well, in principle I could. But I think that that would be highly inappropriate, in bad taste, that I as the accused should be an agent for the Registry who would be looking for the right kind of agency in Belgrade to have this book translated. Secondly, I won't be travelling for years, decades, especially not to Belgrade, I have to do this through an intermediary, whereas the Registry has its own office in Belgrade, the court has its own office in Belgrade, in Belgrade there are many translation agencies that translate documents into foreign languages. That would be very inexpensive. Your translators here are quite spoiled. Their standard is four pages a day; in Belgrade all of this goes a lot faster and the quality is good, too. When I needed a translation of the Statute of the Serb Radical Party, we engaged an agency, they did this work, it wasn't expensive at all, it was a lot cheaper than what you pay your translators here. But the Registry has to do that. If you really insist that I do this, it's not hard for me to do that, but I think it would be inappropriate, in addition to all the work that I'm doing on my defence to work for the Registry, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I've listened to you carefully. So you would be of the opinion that the Registry which has an office in Belgrade could see what can be done locally so that they themselves ask for a price estimate. Why not? But this could also be done by your associates who are there in Belgrade, and as early as tomorrow, they can take the book somewhere to have a price estimate very quickly. It all depends on whether you want a solution very quickly or less so. At any rate, you showed and emphasised that in fact there were two books that are relevant to you in your defence. But whilst I was listening to you, I discovered something else which I hadn't quite realised initially. You had told me so last week, but I did not make the connection. You explained that in the 90 books you had written there were many of them containing speeches that you made as part of your political career at the time and there were also other things, and you indicated so that the Trial Chamber can fully grasp the scope and the extent of your political speeches, if I do understand you well and do not betray your thinking, you believe that the Trial Chamber should have all of your political activity of the time as translated into press clippings, articles, TV shows, interviews, et cetera, and you would easily admit that, yes, it is something important and of quite huge proportions, because if the OTP studied your 90 books the Trial Chamber has not done so. So there is a new question I have to put to you. As you know, trial proceedings here are made up of two stages. There is the Prosecution case and then the Defence case. As part of the Defence case you said that you were going to testify. We understood that very well. However, you, do you plan to call an expert witness; and if so, the expert witness could draft a report based on a summary of all your intellectual or political oeuvre, of your work. Have you planned to do so or not? Indeed, how can you let the Trial Chamber know about the contents and the entire extent of your action because we have three speeches in the indictment, but these three speeches are only minute portion of scores, if not hundreds of writings of yours. So anything that will be missing, how do you plan to introduce that, to tender that, as part of your defence case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, maybe I wasn't clear enough or the interpretation was not accurate clear enough. I don't think that you, as the Trial Chamber, should read all these books; it wouldn't be possible anyway. I informed you that in 2003 I turned over to the Prosecution discharging my obligation of disclosure in advance, I turned over 80 books. The guards brought them into the courtroom, and the Prosecution extracted interviews and speeches out of those books that they thought relevant to the indictment. And from the list of exhibits delivered by the Office of the Prosecutor, I saw that they are full of these speeches. They haven't been given to me, but I suppose they will eventually. I wouldn't ask for many more of those speeches and interviews to be admitted into evidence, but my experts from my expert team, when they were handing over to the OTP notice of special defence they made extracts from these speeches from which we see that I advocated humane treatment of civilians, prisoners of war, observation of international law, and there were a couple of hundred pages. The Prosecution translated all that and maybe they made it available to you in English, because I gave them that in 2003. The Prosecution treats them scornfully, like my propaganda speeches. Second, regarding to the Prosecution expert Oberschall, the Prosecution made available to me an additional text of 240 pages. They made an expertise, an expert report, from the Prosecution and we made our own expert report, taking care not to exceed their number of pages. At the time being it was 240 pages, and I'm planning to give it to you. I have experts lined up, just like the OTP has, one of them has already finished his report and gave it to me on hundred pages about hate speech. It's Dejan Mirovic, a member of my expert team assisting the Defence. I will make that available to you in a couple of days. I am dealing with expert reports, and through them I will avoid the need to translate entire books. However, concerning the two books we were talking about, this is not possible. If it had been possible to write the book "The Roman Catholic Criminal Project of the Artificial Croatian Nation" on a hundred pages, I would have written it on 100 pages rather than on 1.000. I wrote it in prison, here from 2003 to end 2006, I wrote it in long-hand. I can show you the manuscript if you wish. It had been possible on a hundred pages, why would I have written a full 1.000? It wasn't possible. It had to be complete, it had to be relevant, every reference had to be mentioned, and they were mentioned in the body of the text itself. In Serbia a great number of scientific meetings have been held and seminars on that topic. It spurred great reactions in the public, it reflects my ideology. If you want to know that ideology in order to make a fair judgement, that book is necessary; if you don't want that, then there's no need to translate anything at all. It is up to you to decide. I can, as soon as tomorrow, ask my associates to find an appropriate translation agency, but the agency has to sign a contract with the Registry because I cannot bear that cost. I am happy that the book was published in Serbian; I am not interested in English or any other language. I am addressing the public in Serbia. I'm not interested in any other public, especially the Western public because it was from the West that all the evil originated throughout the centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have reassured me because you have told me that your expert drafted 240 pages in line with Mr. Oberschall's report, and I assume that in these 240 pages some passages will pertain to your book. In addition, you also mentioned if the Trial Chamber is satisfied with this that you have planned to call ten expert witnesses. The pending work will be completed very shortly and you will be able to then present this to the Chamber. This clearly demonstrates that you are actively preparing your defence. Perhaps there is something which was badly translated a while ago, something you did not understand properly. What I wanted to say to you that if in Belgrade somebody whom you know, somebody close, your wife or one of your associates or X, Y, Z, anybody, goes to see a translation agency, the agency then prepares an estimate and indicates how much that will be. And then this estimate, which is not a binding document in any way, can then be send to the Registry and the Registry can approve it because the cost is reasonable. And then that problem is solved. You told me that as far as you were concerned it is for the Registry to deal with this. You are quite right, but I would also like to draw your attention to the fact that if you wish to gain time and to make sure that all these pages will be translated, as your book has already been published, you can give us an approximate estimate and then the registry can on the basis of the estimate and according to the amount agree or disagree. This is what I wanted to tell you. Have you understood me well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do that. I can do that as soon as tomorrow and I can inform you maybe as soon as Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That being settled, I shall move on now. As I told you, as a Pre-Trial Judge and now that we have a proper Bench, it is of course right that you should be able to express yourself and you should be able to prepare yourself and to prepare your defence properly. I therefore would like to address another issue, which is, so to speak, a stand-by issue for the time being and that relates to the issue of your associates. You told me - and this was very clearly spelled out by you last time - that your associates remain in Belgrade, will not be here because you felt that there was no reason for you to give to the Registry the name of one of the three associates of yours who is a lawyer and who is a member of the Belgrade bar. You were very clear on this particular point. Since we met last time, I have spent a lot of time thinking about this and I have tried to find a way of settling this issue. In my mind - and I believe my colleagues share the same feeling - in light of the experience of my colleagues also, and in light of the proceedings before this Tribunal, you have a number of issues to contend with and you have demonstrated this. And if you are helped in your work by associates, all the better. As you know, I have handed down a decision which entitles you to have associates that would be paid by the Tribunal, on condition of course that you are unable to pay them. Given that you're indigent, and this is what you have told us at great lengths, you provided us or provided the Registry with all the necessary information, and it was for the Registry if they wanted to ascertain this that it needed to do what was necessary to check this out. At the last Status Conference I did address this issue without belabouring it, and I did say that as part of the cooperation with your country the Registry could turn to the tax authorities to ask what your situation is from a tax standpoint. And if we were then to get a letter from the appropriate ministry, the Registry could then conclude that you are indigent and that therefore all the costs should be borne by the Registry by what is called here legal aid. Now, as a matter of principle, I have no comment to make about this. You have told us that you have done all that is needed. The Registry has told me that they did turn to the tax authorities in question, and they have every reason to believe that as soon as the tax administration of your country responds to their letter, they will be able to see whether you are indigent or not. But that is not what the issue is about. The issue pertains to your associates who are prepared to help you and whether they are going to come here or not. One of your three associates is a lawyer, and I state this once again because we are holding this hearing in open session like we did before. But it is important for everyone to be aware of the fact, to be aware of this. Why is the Registry keen on ascertaining that among your associates one of them is a lawyer? It's not somebody who would be wearing a robe and who would be speaking on your behalf? No. It's because this person is a fully-fledged lawyer and is -- will be given a salary due to his status. He will be -- this is a way of justifying his salary and that the money will not be used for anything else. This is why the Registry is requiring this information because they have to control their funds, and they don't want to be caught and having spent taxpayers' money and international taxpayers' money inadvertently. As you know taxpayers' money when it comes to' international civil servants is discussed at the UN Security Council who provide funding. This is a reason why the Registry is asking you to state that one of your associates - it can be any one of the three - is a fully-fledged lawyer. So it's for you to turn around and say: He is a lawyer. This is something I've told you before. Even if you've given us the names of 25 people who are preparing your defence, these names are listed on the documents which have been officially filed. Only one of these 25 needs to be a lawyer. You just say X, Y, Z is a lawyer, but you must tell this to the Registry, and then I believe that the issue would be settled once and for all. The Trial Chamber has done all it could. I have done all I can to find a solution to this problem, and it would be a shame for you, Mr. Seselj, if for a question of principle which may be justified, that you can't tell us that among those associates, whether it be 25 or 30 of them, that one of them is a fully-fledged lawyer. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, not a single man who is representing himself has to have a lawyer to help him. And as a condition for someone to represent oneself, the only requirement everywhere in the world is to be literate, to read and write, that is considered to be qualification enough, together with a modicum of intelligence. A person has to be moderately reasonable. That's enough. When you have to decide whether I can represent myself, you also have to decide whether I'm bearing any costs or not. Costs are proven by material evidence. You know that other persons have written quite a lot on my behalf. You know that I have made 337 submissions so far. I wrote perhaps a hundred myself, but over 200 were written by other people. Sometimes there are huge studies in which an enormous amount of work was invested, that hasn't been paid to date. I don't know how long my associates are going to continue to work on credit in the hope that one day they will be paid. In future, there will be proof provided of their work. Second, whether they are going to be present in the courtroom or not, they will be present if they are paid for being here, helping me. All my three associates are members of the Serbian parliament, MPs; in order to come here, they would have to resign on their jobs as MPs and they would have to renounce their salaries. And they have to provide upkeep for their families. So that's complicated. Very tendentiously, the Registry is pushing me to have a lawyer in my team. I have several lawyers on my team, but I didn't engage a single one of them because they had a degree in law. I engaged them because they were trusted men and good legal men, whether or not they passed the bar exam. You know from all my submissions that my main legal associate is Zoran Krasic. I don't want to degrade or humiliate Zoran Krasic, who made the greatest contribution to my defence, and appoint someone else who contributed less just because the other person is a lawyer. I don't want to accept that and I don't want to accept such blackmail on the part of the Registry. I didn't have to have a single lawyer on my team. I could easily very soon exclude all lawyers from my team, just because the Registry is behaving this way, and then even formally I wouldn't have any lawyers. My defence consists of good legal men who are willing to follow my instructions and they do so in good conscience, very well, very efficiently, and they are investing a great deal of work. Each of them could have by now gained a Ph.D. if they had worked on their thesis instead of helping me. I can work practically alone, that problem does not exist for me. You know, those who are representing the Office of the Prosecutor here are not a threat, they are not my equals, not in their knowledge of facts, not in their knowledge of basic legal categories. They are simply not up to me. I will have as many assistants as I need to do the work meticulously, to deal with a huge amount of material, or I won't have any. If that is not made possible, I can do it on my own. It was important for me, as important as my life itself, to represent myself, but I'm not going to fight for funds from the Registry. Please don't believe that theory. If the Registry won't give me a penny for my Defence, I'm going to represent myself on my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have just said I knew already, but it's important that my colleagues hear this. Now, you have three associates. When decision on the funding of one of them has to be taken, I mentioned an associate. I didn't talk about a lawyer or a legal officer. I just talked about an associate and the Bench need not look into the qualities of these associates. These are three associates, because I have read everything written by Zoran Krasic so far, and therefore there's nothing more to be said on that score. You have told me, and you're telling me again, and the Bench may perhaps discuss it at a later stage, if your associates come here to help you this will directly impact their situation because if they are MPs they are remunerated as such, and if they come here they quite obviously will not be able to be MPs in Belgrade and defend you here. They would then have to resign of course, and if they resign they need to be paid somehow. They can't just live on hot air. And if they're to be paid, this has to be taken into account when a decision a taken. There is no disagreement on this point between you and the Trial Chamber, it's just a matter of assessing the costs and making sure they're right. The only stumbling block, and that is perhaps something which has not been sufficiently highlighted, is the following. You told me that for psychological reasons, it's Mr. Zoran Krasic who will be your lead counsel, and you don't see why you should appoint anyone else who would act as a lawyer. This I understand full well, and I don't disagree with you as far as this psychological aspect is concerned. But you have said, I will appoint this lawyer, but in fact the three people helping you have already been appointed since you have already given us or given the names to the Registry. So everybody knows who these three people are. So there's no need to appoint anybody anymore since these people are your associates already. So this part of the question has been settled. The only outstanding item which remains to be settled is that the Registry is asking you that one of these people is a lawyer, and this is to comply with the UN rules. And if the person in question - let's assume of course -- this is a hypothetical situation of course, please understand me, let's assume that somebody is being paid and he does something else, he goes on the beach and doesn't do his work, which could be a problem because he's being given money and that could not be substantiated from a legal point of view. Therefore, the Registry needs to be able to explain that the money paid has been paid out as it should and that the Registry is able to monitor this. So now, if we are talking about your three associates, if one of the associates is a fully-fledged lawyer, then according to the code of ethics, would ask the other two to comply with the rules; namely, that one is paid for services rendered and not paid for nothing. And that is the only thing that is important here, and this can be settled very easily, in a split second. You send a document which would read as follows: Registrar, pursuant to the decision handed down by the Trial Chamber, I would like to indicate that Mr. X, who is one of my three associates, is a lawyer in Belgrade. Full stop, that's it. And as far as I'm concerned, that suffices. That doesn't mean that on your team this person is considered to be a lawyer. All the Registry needs is for this person in Belgrade to be a lawyer. He won't be a lawyer whose name will figure on the list of Defence counsel of the Tribunal. He just needs to be a lawyer -- he can be a lawyer in Canberra, in New York, in Belgrade, I don't mind. So you have just about reached the end of a long road, the road has been long for you but it has been long for me too. It hasn't been easy to hand down this decision. Therefore, if you write this short paragraph and you state X is a lawyer in Belgrade, this means that the Registry could then pay the case manager, your three associates, and then the ball can start rolling. So, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you enabled me to get to the end of the road by shortening the road considerably. I was somewhere at the beginning of that road. You removed a very long stretch, many kilometres, now I'm at the end of the road. I was trying to put a little humour into this, I hope it's not appropriate [as interpreted]. Judge, in 2003, I provided information about Slavko Jerkovic and the certificate that he's a lawyer, just as I did for another legal associate that I rejected later for many reasons, I don't want to repeat the reasons. And then in December I provided the information for all three legal associates, and their entire CVs, evidence that one of them is a lawyer, the other one is a lawyer, and the third one is a lawyer together with their career. The Registry is informed of all that. I just don't want to appoint any one of them as lead counsel. The Registry can deal with the problem very easily. All three of them can have equal salaries. I don't want one of them to receive the entire amount and pay the other two. I want each one of them to receive a salary for their own work. If anybody sees them on the beach, I will be the first to ask that person to be stricken off my list because I am very well known for the way I push people who work for me and with me, because I myself invest a lot of effort and work very hard and everybody else who works with me has to follow. If all the three of them have the same salary, the problem is dealt with. Don't tell me that one of them, because he is a lawyer, has to have a higher salary, even double than the others, just like you have a huge difference between lead counsel and co-counsel, the lead counsel has 40.000 euros and the co-counsel 20.000. I don't want the Registry to do this, bargaining and dividing among my associates. All of them must have equal salaries and I will be the first one to strike off anyone who doesn't follow my instructions and who doesn't work hard for their money. The Registry should not be doing all this, complicating things unnecessarily. I don't know if you saw their six-page letter in which they impose impossible conditions. Why did an authorised person, authorised by me, visit Macedonia three years ago to investigate one member of the Registry and her travelling? There's a stamp -- there's a stamp as a result of the Macedonian immigration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... which there is in a dialogue is that in dialogue you are bound to make progress. You've just said two important things. The first important thing is this. You said this - I didn't check - but you said back in 2003 you sent a letter to the Registry, stating that among your associates there was some who were already lawyers, and you even specified that Mr. Jerkovic had been pointed out by you to them as a lawyer because that is the word you filed in his CV, so that is one important thing you said. The other important thing which was very obvious to me, and I thought it was settled, is that among the three associates I never thought of treating one more favourably than the others. The way I saw this is that they had to be paid equally. There's not one in the three people who is the lead associate, as it were, whilst the other two would be the co-associates. And in my mind they would be paid in the same way. Since you are the one in charge, you are the one controlling the associates, since you are the one who recruits them, you can fire them the next day if you so wish. So based on that, you are entitled to say: I want them to be paid equally, as you would have been entitled to say that one has to be paid better than the other one for a specific reason. That was your absolute right. Unfortunately, when the decision was handed down, this was not written into the decision because there was no formal application on your part to request that these people should be paid in the same way. If you had filed a request to the purpose, well, of course I would have gone along with you. So please know in my name - but I believe my colleagues are of the same view, if they're not they can say so - but as far as I'm concerned there is no reason for one of them to be better paid than the others because you are the one who chose your associates because of their skills, their knowledge, and if you decide that they should be paid in the same way, a certain amount then will be granted by the Registry as part of their authority, there's no problem. So we have nearly settled this issue, and this dialogue that we have now initiated makes it possible to better understand what is at hand. The Judges will have an opportunity to discuss this issue, and probably based on what you said we'll convey our position to the Registry. So here again, I think that we can really make headway in giant leaps. Last issue before we address the other items, we may not be able to finish before the break but let me start with this, namely the issue of disclosure pursuant to Rule 68(i). You may know this, but you may not, because it was not translated yet. A few days ago I issued a decision on disclosure of material further to Rule 68(i). In the said decision I reminded that the Prosecution is under the legal obligation to disclose to the accused material within the scope of this Rule. And I recalled in the decision I issued a few days ago that there are these famous 207.000 pages, but in fact there are much less than that because the Prosecutor told us - but I stand to be corrected by Ms. Dahl - in fact we're talking about 17.892, this is from memory, I may be wrong - if I am, you will correct me, Ms. Dahl. But even if there are only 17.892 pages, they cannot all be disclosed overnight. In this decision, I think I managed to identify the problem. Let me set it out. My colleagues have already received the report, but I wish to state this again. Back then - but of course Madam Dahl, Ms. Dahl is in no way responsible, she came in later so she was not responsible for that - but back then the initial Trial Chamber had appointed a stand-by counsel, Mr. Van der Spoel. What would the OTP generally do, not as far as you're concerned, but generally so, the OTP will disclose to the appointed counsel in the format of CD-ROMs, they will disclose relevant material, including those pursuant to Rule 68. I'm not talking now about the (i) or the (ii), I'll do that later. And what happened? The material was disclosed to that lawyer, but at the same time the Prosecution also sent you to your cell the CD-ROMs as well as DVDs. You for your part, you wrote that you would not accept the documents, that material, in electronic format. And you sent them all back. So that's as things stand. Those were the facts. The Judges amended Rule 68 in December 2004 -- sorry, on the 12th of December, 2003, and then it was amended again on the 28th of July, 2004. I was there, so I can testify to that. I was then there at the plenary session amending the rule by making a distinction under Rule 68, under -- between (i) where the Prosecutor will disclose to the Defence everything that is such as to exonerate in part or in -- mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence. That's the little (i). Therefore, the Prosecutor had to implement this. They had to do so knowing that you would have turned down your lawyer and that you were basically representing yourself. But this escaped everybody. I mean, nobody noticed that. The Prosecution deemed, rightly or wrongly, I won't go into that, deemed that they had been used to disclosing to Defence counsel exculpatory material in electronic format; therefore, they went on doing the same thing, fully complying with their legal obligations. But the situation was quite different. You know, when you have a lawyer, no problem whatsoever, but the problem here was that you, you did not want to have counsel; and secondly, and so you wrote, you wanted the documents in hard copy and also translated into B/C/S. When I saw you after the hunger strike and when I was appointed Pre-Trial Judge, I addressed this issue in front of you. I said that I was going to issue a decision ordering the Prosecution to provide to you in hard copy and also translated into B/C/S all this material, because you were right in demanding that they be provided in that format. Because you do not want to use English, you are perfectly entitled not to want to use English, and you wanted documents in your own language. And moreover, you wanted to have them in hard copy, which is fine by me. So the Defence therefore -- you said so, and I issued a decision in this respect. Then we had Ms. Dahl who took over the case, and she said that she fully agreed. Only she said that she was facing a huge problem, which is that there was a huge amount of documents and she said she was willing to do it, but given that the huge amount of documents she couldn't catch up with the back-log overnight and she was asking whether you could provide her with key words. If she had key words she said she could search the 207.000 pages to try and find anything that could be relevant to you. And as part of the search, she disclosed some documents to you. The decision I issued just a few days ago is a reminder of the whole disposition and recalls that in law you are entitled to have in your own language and in hard copy the material pursuant to Rule 68(i) without any problem whatsoever. I also recalled that in order to speed up the process of disclosure, which is going to be time-consuming due to the huge amount of documents, that of course the Prosecution if they fail to do so they will be punished, as it were, but they have to go on with the disclosure, not everything has to be done within one day, it's spread over time and there is no other way to do it, but the Prosecution maybe start based on some key words that you might introduce, you may have some thoughts about this, you could tell the Prosecution, you could tell Ms. Dahl, please can you do this search for exculpatory material for the following key words and they will do the search for you. So this is the system that was generally adopted. I know from reading the press like everybody, and I read everything that is written in Belgrade, some say that you don't -- do not have the exculpatory material. In a way, that is true, you don't have them all, yes, indeed. And the Prosecution has to disclose that to you. There is no doubt about this, but you must understand that Ms. Dahl is unable to scan 2.000, 7.000 documents overnight and find which of them are exculpatory material. My fellow Judges and myself, we have absolutely no part to play in this respect. We cannot say whether a document is exculpatory or not. Whatever you may think of these proceedings, the procedure of disclosure of material is not controlled by the Judges as to the merits of the document. The Judges - and I can tell you this - the Judges do not want to get involved in the disclosure of material. Therefore, it really is up for the goodwill of the Prosecution. They are the ones deciding whether documents are exculpatory or not. This is a right they have under the Rules. We as Judges are not allowed to interfere as per the Rules. So this is basically the situation in this matter. Therefore, the trial is about to start and you still do not have all the exculpatory material, potentially exculpatory material. This is true. I don't deny this. Nobody can deny this. However, this is only the result of a series of poor functioning, and it is only a practical solution. Ms. Dahl and her associates will keep searching for the exculpatory material and yourself -- of course it's not up to you to do the job normally speaking, but maybe it's a good idea. You could use key words and you could guide, you could steer, the Prosecution in their search. Look, Mr. Seselj, let us assume that you have 207.000 pages tomorrow and somebody is asking you to look for exculpatory material, you could say, Well, I need some time, that's the reality, that's the truth of the matter. You must understand that, and you understand that perfectly well. In this decision I issued recently, I ordered in writing that some 3.000 documents be disclosed, they have been identified through the key words provided at the Status Conference of the 4th of July. So that has to be disclosed to you, but if I take out 3.000 out of the 17.892 pages, there still are a number of documents that have not been listed and have not been disclosed. It's time-consuming and this work will carry on through the combined efforts of the Prosecution that goes on with it, and so far there's nothing to make me believe that the Prosecution did not do their work, but it's also through our own efforts because it's a shame to have you participate in this stage of the proceedings whilst the onus is on the Prosecutor. But this is a solution that is helping you for your Defence. So I've said it all. We know the case. We know the ins and outs. You had disclosed this to me. I was totally unaware of this. I remember you got on your feet in a Status Conference and showed me a document in which mention was made of 207.000 pages. So you were the one who revealed this to me. I didn't know that at all, not at all. So this is how things stand. You may have other ideas; if so, spell them out. Last time, if I remember well, you told me the Prosecution has to be punished, but how can I punish Ms. Dahl? She did all that needed to be done so far and she is not responsible for anything. It's not her fault. As I said, it's just a series of bad moments in the proceedings that resulted in this situation. You have the floor, Mr. Seselj, because this is a relevant facet of your rights as an accused. You've expressed yourself at length, but now that I have my fellow Judges with me I'd like them to hear you as well on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Christine Dahl is very guilty of some things, but I will talk about that in a different context later if you allow me to. Now I'm going to restrict myself only to the question that you put. The database of the OTP contains several million pages of text. The predecessor of Ms. Dahl, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, who was Prosecutor on this case, had certain criteria according to which she singled out 207.000 pages from this enormous database of material that is potentially exculpatory. It was identified, it's not some database through which one has to search now. This is material that was identified as potentially exculpatory that has to be submitted to me in its entirety, and then I have to search through it and see what I may find useful and what I may not find useful. That is the core of the matter. Judge, I'm addressing you and your colleagues now, they are trying to portray this to you now, the OTP, that this is some kind of a fundamental database which is supposed to be explored now and then reduced to 17.200. 207.000 pages have already been identified and it's a terrible mistake that they informed the then-Trial Chamber and me that that is what they identified then. I didn't know about that before they informed me in writing. They gave me in writing that they had identified 207.000 pages of exculpatory material, and I'm clinging to that now. And I keep waving that piece of paper in my hands. For me, this is irrefutable evidence. How they are going to get out of this problem because the Prosecution didn't do anything for five years, let them think about that themselves. I am asking for everything. I am asking for 207.000 pages because Ms. Dahl's predecessor identified that already. I have the right to that. I also highlighted another matter. You know that in a few judgements of the Appeals Chamber it is pointed out that the Prosecutor ex officio is a servant of international justice. It is their duty to prosecute and to reveal exculpatory evidence. I can quote, I can cite, from these judgements next time if you want, I have all of that. The Prosecutor has to show you, as the Trial Chamber, that they invested in terms of discharging this important duty the same effort that they invested in my prosecution. They did not prove that until now at all. We can see that in this domain the Prosecution practically did nothing. And the trial begins tomorrow, tomorrow. This enormous work has not been done yet, so what is the consequence? There is no fair trial; without that, it is impossible to have a fair trial. You can analyse other cases, the simple ones and the more or less complicated ones. How much potentially exculpatory material was disclosed in these cases? In some cases it was several hundred thousand pages. I can give you the actual cases concerned. My case is the most complicated one. I am the most terrible war criminal because my alleged war crimes span three present-day states. You do not have any case that resembles that, the most difficult one of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... You said something -- well, I don't have the figures, but you say that you can tell us that in other cases, accused that you probably know of course, since you meet them in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen, that they had received exculpatory documents. And sometimes you talk about several hundreds of thousands of pages. I don't know anything at all. I don't know what's happening in another case, let's say in the Blagojevic trial, I don't know how many documents there were; same for the Milosevic trial, I don't know. But you, you might be able to tell us because you were made aware of those trials in which allegedly the accused received a certain number of documents, because one thing never ceased amazing me when it came applying this rule. If there is a lot of exculpatory material, it's hard to understand why the indictment remains, because if you have exculpatory material or if it mitigates the guilt of the accused nearly automatically, this is bound to have an impact on the indictment against that accused. Well, this is a personal thought in this respect, but you say that as far as you know there are cases where thousands of thousands of pages have been disclosed to the accused, and you say, I've just about got nothing. That's interesting. Could you go into that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Milosevic case, the Krajisnik case, the Martic case, and I think that in this case that you are dealing with now, Mr. Antonetti, there is also an enormous quantity of potentially exculpatory material involved. The six Bosnian Croats, that's what I'm referring to. These are these complex cases involving enormous quantities, but quite simply the Prosecution gave all of this on CD-ROMs, on DVDs, et cetera, and in that way they rid themselves of this problem in obligation. The problem is that in my case they have to do everything on paper and they don't feel like investing money in that. In their June submission that you received, the Prosecution said that they needed 75.000 euro to put all of that on paper. So these are the few cases that I was referring to so you can check. The core of the problem here is that they don't feel like putting all of this on paper and they don't feel like having it translated into the Serbian language, because in other cases the unfortunate lawyers had to sign documents stating that they speak English, although many of them do not, then they received material in English they did not read it and trials went by. Mr. Milosevic made a mistake so already in the beginning he started receiving documents in English. Of course he knew English a lot better than me so he could allow himself to do that on the one hand. Strategically speaking it was a bad mistake. So they continued to deliver all these documents to him in English. That's the core of the problem. In my case everything has to be on paper, everything has to be in the Serbian language, so they have no way out of this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Look, we have to have a break. After the break, I'll give the floor to Ms. Dahl on the Rule 68 issue. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have resumed our hearing. Mrs. Dahl, as far as disclosure issues are concerned, you know as well as I do what all this is about. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, if you think that the Prosecution is in violation of our disclosure obligations, then I would like to know the details of that. Several times during the Status Conferences over the months you have indicated that I proceed at the risk of punishment or sanction, and I want to know if you think we have done something that has defaulted or prejudiced Mr. Seselj. I want to know the particulars because I have acted in good faith and with due diligence at all times and do not consider that we are in default of any of our obligations. I want to indicate that there have been no series of bad moments in this case. The case has been made more difficult by Mr. Seselj's wilful blindness and his strategic and hollow objections to conforming to the rules of practice before this Tribunal. We disagree with the Presiding Judge's recapitulation of the Prosecution's undertakings to try to redisclose - and I emphasise the word "redisclose" - to Mr. Seselj in his capacity as a self-represented accused. I understand our obligation under Rule 68(i) as defined by the decision of this past summer in June to require disclosure in paper, in a language Mr. Seselj understands, of material that falls within Rule 68(i), that is, material within the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor which may suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. We are not hunting for exculpatory evidence in the evidence collection, looking for something that doesn't exist, looking for a needle in a haystack. Looking for something that shows that Mr. Seselj is innocent, when in fact we will prove that he is guilty, is a futile exercise. The Prosecution's undertaking with regard to material that was already disclosed to Mr. Seselj, that he refuses to use, extended to key-word searches from material that he finds material to his -- the preparation of his defence, relevant material, that is, Rule 68(ii). We do not agree that those key words produce exculpatory evidence within the meaning of Rule 68(i). We need to review material and appreciate its relevance to the case; when that happens and we see that it may mitigate his guilt or suggest his innocence, we promptly comply with the order that redefined the Prosecution's disclosure obligations as an accommodation to Mr. Seselj's status as a self-represented accused. This Chamber cannot allow him to use that status to make the proceedings unfair or unfairly delay it. We have undertaken to consider the latest order regarding the so-called 3.000 documents. I need to correct some information about what those documents relate to. Those are documents narrowed from the electronic evidence collection that are within the public portion of the electronic disclosure system. Copies now reside in a case-specific folder for Mr. Seselj. At this stage we are not in a position to implement the Chamber's latest order. We have serious concerns about its legal and factual basis. We have prepared and are now revising a disclosure report concerning Rule 68, but we wish to look at that report in light of the new order. While the order relates to 3.000 documents, this number represents only the product of the first search items that are now on the EDS. It has the potential, if the reasoning is extended to all of the other search items, to apply to many, many more documents that may be relevant to Mr. Seselj's preparations, but until we have reviewed them and identified them as exculpatory under Rule 68(i), we are under, we consider, no obligation to put them into the format that Mr. Seselj prefers. We're looking at the significant resource implications of the order, not just for this case but for the other cases that we have to staff in order to translate documents for the ongoing trials. We may need to seek certification of the decision in order to secure a ruling on the scope of our obligation and its grounding. We also have undertaken the obligation to review the privileged material or the confidential material in the Prosecution's possession, and we are turning our attention first to that so that we can determine whether it can be put on the EDS in its confidential nature, for instance, material received from Rule 70 providers would not automatically go on to the EDS. There are protocols to follow before we can disclose that. Mr. Seselj proceeds from a false premise with regard to the 207.000 documents. Mr. Milosevic accepted electronic disclosure and the material that produced that figure relates to material disclosed in the Milosevic case. It does not represent a determination that it is exculpatory or shows the innocence of Mr. Seselj; it represents material that may be useful to him. And if the Chamber considers that we have done something that has -- that we have done something that has prevented him from preparing, I need that finding and the reasons behind it made now because this trial must be fair and I will do my utmost to discharge the obligations under the resources that this office has and the rules of procedure that this Tribunal operates under. But if you make a wholesale sea change in how things are done, then we need a reasonable opportunity to make sure that Mr. Seselj has what he needs. I say he has already been given what he needs and what the Rules require; he has elected not to use it. That is the right of a self-represented person. They can refuse to use the materials put in front of them, but what they cannot do is bend to their own will and their own strategic objections how the Tribunal operates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you always surprise me when you take the floor. Seemingly you have not read the decision which the Bench handed down on the 5th of November, which is entitled as follows, because before taking the floor you need to be well-informed. Let me read you the title of this decision: Second decision as far as obligations of the Prosecution are concerned, Rule 68(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I shall read you part of this. "Given that during the Status Conference on the 27th [as interpreted] of October 2007 that the question of 207.000 pages that had been disclosed electronically by the Prosecution on the 7th of September, 2007 [as interpreted], pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules was not settled, given that the accused asked for these documents to be disclosed on paper." See at the 23rd of October Status Conference pages 1646, 1647. So please listen carefully. "Given that it is for the Prosecution and the Prosecution only to determine on a case-by-case basis the material to be disclosed and for the accused to have a fair trial. Please refer to Oric and Brdjanin decision. "Considering that the only obligation which is that of the Trial Chamber is to remind the Prosecution of its obligations to provide exculpatory material and that it -- when it knows that the accused is advised of this and to sanction" -- let me repeat. I was going too fast. "Considering that the sole obligation which is that of the Trial Chamber is to remind the Prosecution of its obligation and to order the disclosure of documents that could mitigate the guilt of the accused when is knows that the accused has knowledge of these documents and if there is a failure to do this, to sanction this. "Considering that, as far as this matter is concerned, the Prosecution has stated during the last Status Conference, having identified some 3.000 documents, thanks to the key words provided by the accused on the 4th of July, 2007, Status Conference, given that these key words had been identified by the accused when he had stated that the 207.000 documents could potentially be exculpatory. "Considering that having conducted research and based on the key words provided by the accused, the Prosecution is aware of the existence of 3.000 documents, approximately, that could mitigate wholly or in part the guilt of the accused or that could, in fact, affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. "Considering that the decision of the 7th of June, these documents need to be provided to the accused in hard copy and in a language he understands as soon as possible for the foregoing reasons and pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules and the decision handed down on the 7th of June orders that the Prosecution discloses, as soon as possible, on paper and in a language that the accused understands, these 3.000 documents which the Prosecution has identified thanks to the key words provided by the accused." This is what the Bench stated on the 5th of November, so don't talk about sanctions. We haven't reached that stage yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is apparent from the transcript and the language in the decision that there is a misunderstanding about what we consider those 3.000 documents to be. At the last Status Conference we returned from break and you had put the question to me whether we had a record of how many documents we had disclosed since the June order to the accused under Rule 68(i). I told you the number of receipts, and I told you approximately how many documents were covered by each receipt. Unfortunately, we do not keep records of the total number of documents under Rule 68(i) that we disclose. I failed to make clear at the Status Conference when I switched subjects and then described what we had put on to the electronic disclosure system, I regret not making clear that I was switching subjects. We do not consider the key words that Mr. Seselj provides and his assertion that those topics yield exculpatory evidence mean that it is, in fact, exculpatory evidence within our view. If he were to declare key words, he could grind our ability to search on his behalf, as a courtesy to his preparations, to a halt. He could decide to say that anything Croatian is a key word for his defence, anything Muslim is a key word for his defence. It is the obligation of the Defence to determine for himself what he wishes to search on and how he wishes to prepare his defence. To that end, we are, under the Rules, authorised to make available in electronic format relevant collections of material. Just as with all of the Defence counsel practicing before the Tribunal, I ensured that Mr. Seselj has that same facility available to him. And I went one further. I am prepared to give him a paper index in a language he understands indicating the search results to allow him easy access into the electronic collection. His associates could also have an account, access, but the fact that he brands a particular word or a combination of words as exculpatory does not bring it within the confines of Rule 68(i), and I do not think that we can expand the translation burden and the burden of production to the paper which Mr. Seselj wants. What we are really talking about is who bears that burden consequent on his refusal to make use of the tools that are available to him. It's coming down to who will print the paper. He is quite eager to have his associates help him when it suits his purposes, and quite eager to shift the burden back to the Prosecution knowing that it's untenable, just like he has tried to bring in thousands of pages of text that represents his brand of bellicose nationalism as a defence here. He is also trying a strategic objection to the production of disclosure material. We will prepare our response to the order and look at what it entails, but it must be kept in mind that those 3.000 documents represent only the first instalment of search results that our information support unit has conducted at my direction, and there will be a cascading effect on this case and the work entailed by that order if it applies, as it appears to, that we must now print and translate material that is relevant to the preparation of his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to the key words, Mrs. Dahl. At the Status Conference Mr. Seselj had said that he was willing to help "the Prosecution to look up exculpatory material." And he had quoted, for I remember, the group called White Wasps and White Eagles -- Yellow Wasps and White Eagles and if you'd like to refer to this, he had stated that people who had committed crimes had nothing to do with him. So, quite rightly, he feels that all the documents that quote the Yellow Wasps could be of interest to him which is, of course, a theory he is presenting. These people had nothing to do with him so this is what he was asking for. So by using the key words which he provided, I had understood that the research had led to some 3.000 documents or so, I don't know the details of all of this. Second point, Mr. Seselj is defending himself and this right has been granted to him by the Trial Chamber. I cannot in any way question the accused's right to defend himself. Secondly, Mr. Seselj does not wish to or does not speak English or French; those are languages he does not speak. Therefore, he wishes to have all these documents in his own language. Notwithstanding the case-law of this Tribunal, you just need to turn to the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights. In other words, any accused or defendant should have all the documents in his own language. Also, you are still saying that he should nonetheless resort to electronic disclosure. Mr. Seselj has always said that he would refuse any form of electronic disclosure. I stand to be corrected, but that was one of the reasons why he went on a hunger strike which led to the Appeals Chamber reviewing the whole case. Therefore, Mr. Seselj says, I would like to have a hard copy version of all the documents because I do not use a computer. This would be unheard of, to impose on someone the use of a computer. Let us imagine that Mr. Seselj can't either read or write, in that case the Prosecution will turn around and say, Well, he needs to use a computer. There is something askew here, as you can see. So the Trial Chamber's not going to rule on any sanctions to be taken, and as I've told you, you are not held responsible for this. I have reminded you, but perhaps you've found it difficult to understand. Maybe I've spoken too fast. Initially the problem was due to the fact that all these documents were sent in an electronic form to his lawyer, and he had then refused all these documents. That's where the problem stems from, and if we are -- whether it be a British lawyer or an American lawyer, so be it, but if the documents are being sent to someone who doesn't speak the language then we have a problem. The documents, therefore, need to be sent to him in B/C/S and in hard copy form. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution has taken the floor. You may have something to say about this. Before moving on to another topic I shall give you the floor again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad that you as the Trial Chamber are so tolerant towards Mrs. Christine Dahl as the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, even when she's using insulting words like "hollow objections," "wilful blindness," et cetera. I'm happy because I like this kind of tolerant situation more than some other kind of situation where Ms. Dahl would strictly abide and -- by the rules of decency, courtesy, and act courteous. I don't think it's a hollow objection when they say the Prosecution is not hunting for exculpatory evidence because they can prove that the accused is guilty. It's a wrong understanding of the role of the Prosecutor. The role of the Prosecutor is to look for the truth, to establish the truth, not to look for an outcome where the Trial Chamber would find the accused guilty at any cost. That's why they are prepared to use false witnesses. They brought recently to The Hague my defence, my potential defence witnesses, in order to intimidate them. That is an essential misunderstanding of her function by herself. That is why she is incapable of doing her job which facilities my defence considerably. I will much more easily cope with this kind of Prosecutor than with somebody smart who knows the law and who knows their role and who would act from that understanding. Only a smart person in her place could be a threat to me; she cannot be a threat to me. Second, she identified --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 207.000 pages of exculpatory material and the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, you will have the floor soon, but let Mr. Seselj finish and then you can reply. He didn't interrupt you when you were on your feet. So as a matter of courtesy, let him finish and then you can respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want some ground rules set, please. I do not think that his argument which is insulting to me is appropriate, and that is why it needs to be stopped instead of being replied to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please resume, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm doing all of this out of my wilful blindness that you established and because I'm only making hollow objections, that's something you noted. Why -- what are you afraid of then when I want to confirm my wilful blindness or the hollowness of my objections. Then you jump up like a jack-in-the-box and complain that I'm insulting you. No, I'm not insulting you. I'm only repeating what you said at my expense. 207.000 pages were identified by the OTP as potential exculpatory material and they signed it. I want all of it. Judge, you said something before the break that was very interesting. If all that were really exculpatory, the Prosecution could abandon all the charges against me. It doesn't necessarily have to be exculpatory material. It is only on certain criteria that the Prosecution thought it could be and it is up to me to decide whether I can use it or not, whether it's potentially useful or not. That is the obligation of the Prosecutor, and it's another obligation of the Prosecutor to carefully and meticulously look for the truth. I, who am representing myself, have only one role here: To defend myself successfully. But the role of the Prosecutor is completely different. It is not their job to have me declared guilty at any cost. The job of the Prosecutor is to find the truth, even if I am acquitted as a result, because they should not consider it as a defeat if they find the truth. It's a defeat for me if I'm found guilty, but to this day nobody has appeared who could explain this for the Prosecutor. I would be happy if I managed to edify her a little. She says that I introduced thousands of pages of my nationalism into potential evidence. I have no other purpose here. The only thing I want is to show that this nationalism cannot be identified with the crimes. It didn't stimulate crimes, it is not the cause of crimes, nor is it in any connection with those crimes which were objectively perpetrated. That is my role here, and why would I be ashamed of that role? As you said, Judge, as far as that exculpatory material is concerned, it is not known in advance that it is exculpatory. It has to be checked for its exculpatory value. But the Prosecution has to make it available to me so that I can check it and so that you can evaluate it. The Prosecution has never tried to prove that the Prosecutor as an officer of international justice invested equal effort into looking for the truth and administering justice. The Prosecution has to show their objectivity; I don't. I don't have to be objective at all. I am very, very subjective, but they cannot have a role equal to mine. They have to be impeccable in their objectiveness, and if they manage to prove my guilt, fine. Now they say they are not obliged to hunt for the truth, that's the interpretation I heard, they're not obliged to hunt. Are we in some hunting story here if we are going to recount hunting stories and the Prosecution is very inclined to that. You know what kind of stories they are? The hunting stories in Serbian national tradition and I suppose in your countries as well, hunting stories are false stories, lies, bragging. And unfortunately all the stories told by this Prosecution here are the same. I request, I demand, exculpatory material and I will continue to do so until the end of this trial and I will continue to demand these 207.000 pages. As far as key words are concerned, I can give the key words to the Prosecution only when I get those 207.000 pages, and then they can continue to search using the key words. You see what else the Prosecution is using here? They say if this material is about Yellow Wasps or about the Guards Corps of the Serbian Renewal Movement of Vuk Draskovic, then it's not necessarily exculpatory. It's not exculpatory because it's their case that I'm responsible for the crimes of the guard, of the Yellow Wasps of the White Eagles, the Arkan's men. They put it in the indictment that I'm responsible for the crimes of all the Serbian forces because all the Serbian forces are involved in the joint criminal enterprise. That is the trouble of the Prosecution. They were not able to substantiate and specify any charge they laid against me, that's why they set the context so broadly that it's impossible. They ascribe to me, in fact, all the crimes from the Serbian side. I am prepared to answer for all of them, but then it has to be put in writing. Why did they choose these few? They didn't they write in everything? This ignorance of the international criminal law and the basic legal categories prejudices me. They won't give me exculpatory material. It is obvious from the conduct of Mrs. Dahl that they have no intention of disclosing it. They want me to look for exculpatory material myself, on my own. They want me to do their job. You have to prove that your translators and your typists were engaged by you equally in prosecuting me, in trying to prosecute me, and in trying to find exculpatory material. You have to prove that, otherwise your whole situation is untenable, your whole premise is untenable. You really are acting as a hunter. You want to shoot someone down. Maybe you managed in some other trials. In this trial, the hunted -- the hunter will become the prey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, first of all, let us try to remain calm and serene. Justice has to be done in utmost serenity. Secondly, unfortunately for the Prosecution, there are documents showing that the accused -- and unfortunately you were not present. I am saying this once again. So the accused was informed that as part of the exculpatory material there was -- there were 207.000 documents. That's what he was told. I think that was a mistake made by the counsel for the Prosecution before you. They didn't realise this and they should have said that there was a mistake, that it was not 207.000 pages. Unfortunately, Mr. Seselj at the last Status Conference and we have a letter from the previous OTP representative, there was a letter that was shown with 207.000 exculpatory pages.
