So rightly or wrongly - the Trial Chamber is not here to make a determination as to the way he is going to represent himself - he says, I want to have those documents. That's what he says. So facing that I told you, but my fellow Judges share my view, 207.000 documents, it is huge, it is colossal task, so how are we going to handle it? We already have an answer. You do your level best. Secondly, with the key words you disclose to him whatever you can disclose to him. You keep disclosing the documents as they come up if you think it is exculpatory material, and that's the way it's going to proceed. Listening to you and whenever you speak, just as I listen to you, just as I listen to Mr. Seselj, I try to understand, of course there could be translation errors, interpretation errors, but I do try to understand what you want to say. And my impression is that you say your position is that you're going to disclose those 207.000 pages in electronic format to Mr. Seselj, let him manage, let him find his way, and then this is something you said you're willing to give him an index of the documents to help him in his search even if he can give you further key words for you to keep on searching. So that is your position. I don't know whether you talked this out with Ms. Carla del Ponte, but we might have her come over here so that she also can give us an explanation. But the problem is that an accused was told that there was a certain amount of exculpatory documents and he wants to have them in his own language and he wants to have them in hard copy. That's it. That's the extent of the problem. I'm not talking about sanction. You said what sanction or punishment. No, I never said that. Why punish you or sanction you whilst you've inherited this case, and you are in no way responsible for things that were done before you were here. Since you've taken over this case, you endeavour to do the best you can for him to get these documents. So do not be trapped in any attitude. It may be wrong, but I seem to understand that you want to remain within this no man's land in which the accused would not be apprised of these documents, well, that's your choice. Last time I told you there was another solution, it might be a complicated one. We're talking about 207.000 pages. You have interns. Why not ask them to have them printed -- of course you have to check -- I think that there may be another problem. Unfortunately, maybe some day the Judges will understand this problem in a plenary meeting. There may be in the 207.000 pages documents that are only in English that have not been translated into B/C/S. Therefore, the accused wants them to be translated into B/C/S, and that's another problem, isn't it? So that's it. I mean, there -- there's a piling up of problems, in fact, and problems are different in nature. The first one that is really -- cannot be avoided is the issue of him having the documents in B/C/S, his language, even if it is in electronic format, assuming that he agrees to the electronic disclosure. But there is one thing that he's not going to agree with is to have the documents in English, so that's another problem. The second problem, but he's been saying so for years, he wants to have them in hard copy because that's the way he works. Ms. Dahl, do you have anything to add? I don't know. We are trying to arrive at solutions, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I join you in that work. I do not wish Mr. Seselj to remain in no man's land and it is not my intention that he remain ignorant of these documents. I will reiterate they are immediately available to him, but he is choosing not to make use of them. His right of self-representation is not unlimited, and I will propose another solution for your consideration. This solution I proposed also with regard to the transcription project which I think warrants discussion today. And this is that his right of self-representation must not be allowed to unfairly delay the trial or impair its fairness over all. It can be limited to a minor extent to require him to make access to documents through the use of a qualified language assistant so that he can read what is in English without undue delay. That is a solution I would like the Chamber to consider as it looks at what the translation burdens are consequent upon his election to represent himself and his insistence on a particular language and format of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this solution you propose, Ms. Dahl, indeed I believe that you realise that there is a problem. Mr. Seselj, presently we're faced with the following situation. You have CD-ROMs containing 207.000 pages, and we do not know at all - I do not know at all, neither do my fellow Judges, what there is in those pages. And the solution suggested might be the following. You would have a "language assistant" who you would choose yourself, somebody who understands English and B/C/S and really is under your orders, paid by the Tribunal of course, and that person under your control and authority could use the CD-ROMs, open them, use them on a screen, sees whether it's in English or not, whether the translation is there or not, so that person would do all that work, following which -- of course the outcome of that work is conveyed to you because this is all under your supervision, and this person would then identify the documents. Let me take an example, haphazardly. Let's imagine that this person electronically views the document and sees that there's one on Vukovar, which is in the indictment, and this person says to you, I found a document on Vukovar, an order or a report, UN report -- well, anything, and he conveys that to you. You, you know your file, you know your case, and you tell him, This is not interesting or, Yes, it is interesting. So this is a document that might be relevant under Rule 68. The Prosecution is then informed of the fact that you want that document, and this work would continue throughout the proceedings and from dawn to dusk this person works behind the screen, identifies pages, says that to you, and upon your instructions that is linked with the key words, the Prosecution would provide to you on hard copy and in B/C/S would provide the documents to you. That's just a thought as expressed by the Prosecution personally. It might be interesting as much as you would have somebody to assist you, somebody who's remunerated by the Tribunal, but you can regard that person as trustworthy because you would appoint them yourself and that person would work on the documents, process them, and would ask you what to do with them. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously, Judge, I would have to deal with the question that you put concerning the other cases where there was such a large amount of potentially exculpatory material in accordance with Rule 68. I mentioned a few cases, and then considerably after that Ms. Dahl said here, if you noticed, that these 207.000 pages of potentially exculpatory material had already been disclosed to Mr. Milosevic as potentially exculpatory material, but that it was a lot easier there for the Office of the Prosecutor because Mr. Milosevic received documents in electronic format and in the English language -- well, maybe they wanted to make their own work easier. So automatically they transferred these 207.000 pages to me. With the exception of Kosovo, the indictment against Mr. Milosevic and the indictment against me coincide to a great degree. They wanted to make life easier for themselves, and they got all messed up in their own irresponsibility and their own incompetence. Now this is termed identified pages, 207.000 of them at that. So I'm being asked to do the work of the Prosecutor. I am searching for potentially exculpatory material all over the place and there is quite a lot of that here already; however, I cannot do the work of the OTP. They have to identify what in their view is potentially exculpatory material and they have to submit that to me. Not have me do that for them and then leave it to their good will as to whether they want to translate something for me and put it on paper. I cannot accept that. I would like to draw your attention to yet another thing. Ms. Dahl towards the end of her remarks said that the right to self-representation is not unlimited and cannot delay the trial. In respect of transcripts from other trials. In addition to this problem of potentially exculpatory material according to Rule 68(i), there is another problem that's much bigger than that. And now we just see the tip of this problem the way we would see the tip of the iceberg, namely, the fact that the Prosecutor intends to bring into evidence an enormous quantity of transcripts from other cases, testimonies of witnesses who are supposed to appear here and that appeared in other trials, an enormous quantity, and all of this is in English. They translated very little for me so far. What they gave me over the past few days is negligible in respect of the quantity of material that they are supposed to be dealing with. They don't feel like translating this into Serbian and they say that my right to self-representation cannot be unrestricted. They want me to receive that in English or at least they want me to tolerate having the Judges admit this into the court record and they want me to act disinterested. You will see that there are problems that are much bigger than the Rule 68 problems. The Prosecution is not trial-ready. The Trial Chamber is ready, I am ready, but the Prosecution is not ready because they have not met not a single one of their obligations. I cannot do the work of the Prosecution. I already have too great a burden to shoulder on my own. They have resources that are far greater than mine and they have to do that. Then you have to assess on the basis of my objections whether they did do this in accordance with the rules or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I shall come back to the second part regarding the testimony or transcripts that the Prosecution would seek to tender into evidence, but you did not quite answer this proposal. We all agree, it is up to the Prosecution to prove and to disclose material under 68(i). Everybody agrees; there's no doubt about this. The only problem is that the Prosecution is not in a position to do that work for the various reasons I have already listed. However, the Prosecution and the Judges do not want you to be harmed or prejudiced because you are entitled to a fair trial, it is an absolute right, and on the other hand there's also the principle of equality of arms. You must be given the same possibilities as the Prosecution. In addition to that, the Judges are Judges who could not as far as I'm concerned, but I think that is true also for my fellow Judges, who could not accept to be part of a farce, a mock trial, where there would be a trial with no representation or no defence by the accused, where there would be no possibility for the accused to enjoy the rights given to him by the Rules and the Statute, that would be unacceptable to me. So taking all these factors into account, taking into account the fact that I do not want to have the feeling that you are disadvantaged, there is one practical solution not envisaged by the Rules, but you are a unique case in the history of this Tribunal since you are the first to defend yourself. Milosevic was in another situation. You are very much the first one, so since you are a unique case we have to find a unique solution. And one of the possible solutions - and I said that earlier on - this is an obligation which the Prosecution has to discharge. However, they cannot do it now. And on several occasions Ms. Dahl mentioned the problem of resources. So one of the solutions would be for this -- this man that you trust could process the electronic documents, tell you which documents to identify, and you would then say whether you want that document in your language and in hard copy or not. It's far from being an ideal solution, I understand. But, you know, between nothing and something, you may as well go for something that is practicable. So this could be a way of making headway, you could choose that person, a person you would totally trust that would do the work for you. I would going to be day or night, but just about, they can meet with you and see what can be done with specific documents. Ms. Dahl agrees that the Registrar will find no problem, he will pay for this person, but it is really up to you, your good will. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please don't expect me to express such goodwill that I'm going to take over the work of the Prosecutor. I don't have a person who I trust this way. I would have to do it by myself and I cannot. The OTP has to do that. With the best of intentions, I cannot meet this recommendation of yours because I don't take it to be a request. I take it to be a recommendation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I take due note of your answer. There is another problem that you raised and I wanted to raise myself. The Prosecution is bound to seek to tender transcripts of testimony of some 49 witnesses, individuals who have testified in prior cases and whose testimony amounts to, according to my figures, 245 days of testimony. Mr. Seselj, just to give you an idea of what it represents, it is now nearly 5.00 and we are close to 56 pages of record. By 7.00 there will be 100 pages. In other words, one day of hearing represents 100 pages. 245 days, so you multiply that by a hundred, and this means that you would have 24.500 pages in English for the time being, the transcript is only in English, and that would be the transcript of those witnesses' testimony. I understood that you said earlier on that testimony, the transcript, would have to be in your own language as well because this would be regarded as Prosecution evidence, so it has to be in your language. That's an enormous problem, a colossal one. What are we going to do? To have 24.500 pages of transcript translated into your own language. That's quite a task, a daunting one, way beyond the capacity of the Tribunal as things stand -- unless of course the Prosecution would give up the transcripts, would not use them, and would make do with the viva voce witnesses they have with the transcript when they appear. So, Ms. Dahl, am I wrong in what I've just set out with regard to the transcript issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, a little bit. The transcript issue -- we would have to decide not to call the witnesses at all. The Rules require disclosure of prior testimony under Rule 66(A)(ii). The Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case decided in September of 2000 that when the Prosecution calls a witness for a second time, then the prior testimony from the earlier case is a witness statement that has to be disclosed as part of the pre-trial disclosure package. It would be unfortunate if the transcription burden meant that we couldn't present the case or had to do without critical evidence simply because the witness has testified before. So the problem is a little bit larger. We can't solve it by shrinking the presentation of evidence; it really is a disclosure obligation fashioned under the Rules to apprise the accused of the nature of the Prosecution's case and present him with the relevant body of material, that would be the witnesses' utterances of the crime that he's reporting or the victimisation that he suffered or the events that he observed. I can't, as a Prosecution, pick and choose which parts of that body of evidence of his recollections uttered in court or during an interview to leave out or to reduce the burden on the Defence, that's really their task to decide how much of it, for instance, to cross-examine somebody on it if they misrecall in their second appearance before the Chamber a minute detail. The Defence may decide at that point to challenge the witness's credibility, their ability to perceive events, if they have some problem like that. So it's -- the scope of the problem is not defined by what evidence we will tender per se, it's defined by the fact that the witness has made a previous appearance in the Chamber and because so many perpetrators contributed to the same unfortunate event as each individual perpetrator is tried, sometimes witnesses make multiple appearances here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mrs. Dahl has just raised a real issue. She has no room to manoeuvre. I shall pick up on what she said and supplement what she has said. Mr. Seselj, I don't know whether you have the Rules in front of you. I know you know the Rules by heart, so Rule 66 of the Rules states that the Prosecution is under the obligation to disclose to the accused, pursuant to Rule 66(A)(i), copies of all of the statements when the latter have been annexed to the indictment when the indictment was confirmed. So that's no problem. You've received that. However, as far as (A)(ii) is concerned, this paragraph stipulates that the Prosecution should also provide copies of the statements of all the witnesses which the Prosecution intends to call to testify. So you know as well as I do, the Prosecution has every intention of calling a number of witnesses who have already testified in other cases, in the Milosevic case amongst others, and the Prosecution, in compliance with this rule and in compliance with case-law that stems from Kordic and Blaskic, those two cases which I am about to sum up. In Kordic, the Defence wanted to be provided with a statement provided in the Blaskic case. This witness was a protected witness. The Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case presided over by Judge Jorda at the time had decided that what pertained to Rule 70 would not be disclosed to the Defence, but what did not pertain to Rule 70 could be disclosed to the Defence. And this decision was taken on the 24th of November, 1999, unless I'm mistaken. Five days later, on the 29th of November, the Trial Chamber in Kordic presided over by Judge May handed down a decision that stated that in the Kordic case the accused needed to be -- needed to be provided with the testimonies of the Blaskic case. This was then referred to the Appeals Chamber, and based on the decision which Mrs. Dahl mentioned, the Appeals Chamber recalled that pursuant to Rule 66 the statements need -- needed to be provided, or rather, testimonies heard during a case and that needed to be disclosed to the accused in another case. Based on this, Mrs. Dahl is telling us that, normally speaking, she should disclose all of this to you, needs to communicate all of this to you. Nonetheless, if a protected witness is coming, this has to be notified 30 days before the witness's testimony. And then, as a rule, she is under the obligation of disclosing this to you. So if we have 245 days of testimony and 100 pages, that's 24.500 pages all in all, based on this. As you know, the transcripts which you see on the screen before you are in English. We could have had one part of the screen in French and one part in B/C/S. Initially, according to what I was told, when the trial started we had the transcripts in both languages, in both English and French, and for some mysterious reason we did away with the transcripts in French, which means we now only have the English transcripts. It's a shame at the time we did not have the transcript in all three languages; then we wouldn't have had a problem. Now, these 24.500 pages are in English, and in your language you have the audiotapes which are in a DVD form. This is how things stand, Mr. Seselj. So it would be interesting for me and my colleagues, in light of this problem, to know what your point of view is. You don't have to tell us what your position is today because we have not officially been seized of this issue yet. We have received no motion to that effect, but this is something which might arise in the future. So it is important to pre-empt this. This is why we have a Status Conference and this is why it is a good idea to mention it now. I'm sure you have spent some time thinking about this, but maybe Mrs. Dahl would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this transcription issue arises with regard to witnesses who are not protected by the late disclosure as well. So it is to characterize it as pertaining to witnesses for whom there is a delayed disclosure order, unfortunately makes the issue narrower than it is in fact. We have proposed to solve the problem by ensuring that all of the transcripts are disclosed sufficiently in advance of the witness's appearance so that Mr. Seselj has them available to him in transcribed form, but it's not only those who are the beneficiaries of a protective measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let's look at this from a practical point of view without quoting any names. A witness who will come to testify in December, let's say, I don't know whether this witness has already testified in another case. If he has already testified in another case, you will send Mr. Seselj the transcript of what he has said in his testimony in the other case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course, you know, the optimal view of disclosure of witness evidence is that it is completed before the evidence commences at all so that the accused has a fulsome view of the nature of the Prosecution case, but we intend to order the nature of our witnesses so that people for whom there is a great transcript load, so to speak, meaning that their duration of prior testimony is four or five days or so, that they come at the end of the case so that we can get the transcripts completed before their appearance, but we are unable to complete all of the transcripts before the appearance of the first witness. And in recognition of that, we propose to call when we commence evidence in December an expert witness who's never testified before the Tribunal at all, and so therefore his disclosure should be complete before the commencement of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, therefore you have just told me now that the first witness who is going to testify will be an expert witness. The expert report has been provided, he has that report, so that's not a problem. Who is this expert witness whom you intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We thought it would be appropriate to begin with Dr. Oberschall, who will give us an overview of Mr. Seselj's propaganda and describe the crisis mentality of his public rhetoric and that contribution to the collective violence that engulfed the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, so we have a series of items here. This is why it's so important to hold a Pre-Trial Conference. First of all, we have one problem is how the prior testimonies and transcripts should be provided to you, testimonies of people who have testified in other cases, like in the Milosevic trial, for instance, so you should be aware of these. Disclosure will be made, I believe, either electronically or, if need be, you will have a hard copy in English. But unfortunately, you will not have a hard copy in B/C/S. You have the translation maybe, in certain cases that will be the case, maybe not, I don't know. But in the event that the Prosecution would not be able to translate some of the testimonies made in other trials, what would your position be? This may require some time, therefore Mrs. Dahl feels it would be better then to start in December. I'm mentioning this to you today. This would be during the second week of the month of December because the Bench is otherwise busy. We will meet again tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. The first witness is Witness Oberschall, who will come to testify on the 11th and 12th and 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have to be provided all the transcripts of all the witnesses that the Prosecutor intends to call in this case and the persons who testified in other cases previously. That is based on current jurisdiction and also Rule 66(A)(ii). You did your calculations right, and I continued it. You said 49 witnesses, there's probably going to be more than that because the Prosecution did not bear in mind here the delayed disclosure witnesses. There's 16 of them, I think ten a month before the beginning of trial and six before the beginning of their testimony, but that's a different problem altogether and I'll refer to it later. So your calculation was 245 days is 24.500 pages. Now, you are looking for a possibility for me to receive all of this in DVD format and to listen to that, 245 days is 1.000 hours. I'd need 125 days just to listen to all of this. Now, you consult a psychiatrist and see whether anyone can remain sane if they sit with headphones on for 125 days listening to some kind of court proceedings. I don't think that anyone could do that. I always boast of my express mental health whenever I can, but even I could not take that. What can I do after 125 days like that? Can I remember all that? Can I cross-examine on all that? I can be prepared for cross-examination only if I read that and if I made my own notes on the margins. I'm going to show something to you now. My statement, statement of the accused, on Thursday I looked at the indictment and the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor and I wrote on the margins everything that I'm going to tell you on Thursday. I cannot work in any other way. I did not write a speech. I'm just going to use this. I'm going to follow what they wrote and I am going to crush them. I'm going to break them. That is what I'm going to do. I have to prepare for cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses in the same way; in order to prepare, I have to have everything on paper. Now, you want me to have headphones on for 125 days and to listen to all of that. Really, if I were to agree to that, what would happen afterwards? Afterwards, I should pretend to be ready to cross-examine them, after 125 days? I wouldn't remember anything that I had heard. Well, perhaps some witty observations maybe. If I were to have this on paper, I would be able to distinguish between the important and unimportant on the margins, I would write down my own remarks, and then I would be ready to cross-examine. Then I can compare what a particular witness said in one case, what he said in another case, and what he said yet in a third case. There are witnesses here who appeared in different trials. I have more to say but if you're going to interrupt me well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to interrupt you, but just an additional comment I'd like to make. Let's take any case before this Tribunal. We have an accused, we have a lead counsel and another counsel, there are two lawyers and three or four assistants. So in a standard -- on a standard defence team there are five people. I'm not talking about you. So what do these people do? They share out the workload. So you are alone. Nobody is challenging you that right. This is why it's so important for you to have associates working with you because, Mr. Seselj, if we reach the moment when your associates will be here present in the courtroom or in Belgrade, this is a suggestion I'm making, this is how they could work. Let's assume that a witness comes to testify, let's assume that he has already testified in the Milosevic trial and that there are five [as interpreted] pages of transcript, you of course won't put on your headsets and listen to the 500 pages. But members of your team could do this work and you would not need to do it, and they could tell you that they have listened to the transcript, that they have summarized it, and that the witness in question has said so-and-so regarding particular issues. And they will let you know. Then when it is time for you to cross-examine the witness, your associates have done the preparatory work for you and you will come to realise and this is something you will realise very soon, that you will have an avalanche of documents, a great number of witnesses, swathes of documents, and then more witnesses, and if you are alone you might be able to face up to this in the beginning, but over time you will be overwhelmed completely. Because -- this is from experience and I'm sure my fellow Judges will say the same, every experienced Judge and sometimes when a witness comes to testify there are five documents that are being adduced, so you have to read all these documents beforehand, you check what this witness has said in other cases, thus this represents a huge amount of work. A witness can come on a Monday, another witness can come on a Tuesday, and for both you have to read 50 documents each. So if you are going to be on your own, how will you manage this? You know the case back to front I'm sure, but at some point, in light of the great number of documents, the transcripts, the Prosecutor will say, Witness X, this is what he says on page 24.500 of his testimony. So of course you are entitled to represent yourself. This is a right that has been granted to you, and I'm definitely not challenging that, but you will have to be helped because it will be very difficult for you to deal with all of this on your own. It will be much more than 24.500 pages. It will be very difficult for you to handle all of that on your own, given that, and Mrs. Dahl has told us and I believe, now I am sincerely convinced, that these testimonies will be translated. Some will be translated, and I am sure that Mrs. Dahl will speed up the translations of these documents, which also represents a huge amount of work. That's why the first witnesses that will come to testify will have translated documents. This is why Witness Oberschall will be called first because his report has been translated. Then we will have the three-week winter recess and we'll resume again in January. So you will have another month to prepare yourself. I know that you have been preparing yourself for years, but you will then have an additional months. But you will reach a time when you will be overwhelmed by all of this. Now, as far as the Oberschall witness -- Witness Oberschall is concerned, what do you have to say about him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not doubt my energy. If I get everything on paper and in the Serbian language, then it's my problem how I'm going to prepare. If I do not prepare successfully enough, then it is my problem only, yet again. However, it is for you as the Trial Chamber, for you and your colleagues, that I receive this material on time and that this material is on paper and in the Serbian language, nothing more than that. If the OTP is not in a position to achieve that, then the question arises what it was that the OTP did over these past five years, why did they not start preparing this on time? They lost five years and now they cannot catch up. There is just one solution for that, for them to give up on such witnesses. They have to bear the consequences, not me. I find it unacceptable to have a single witness appear here if I did not receive his statement and all his testimony from all other cases, because this would constitute a grave breach of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If the Prosecution is not in a position to ensure all of that, so much the better. It's only better for me if they cannot do that. Let them give up on that witness. Let them reduce the number of 105 witnesses to 50 witnesses or 40 witnesses, easier for them, easier for me. What they want is to achieve a maximum result with the least bit of effort, and then they want me to do their work. No way. The problem is far greater than what you referred to here. May I remind you that there is a large number of people who in relation to my case were heard as potential suspects. So some of them agreed to be witnesses, whereas others after these interviews refused. The Prosecution is duty-bound to submit all these transcripts to me, too. For one person they tried to give me a DVD yesterday, but I refused. There's a large number of such people. They have transcripts in English, and I do not have the transcripts in Serbian and I'd have to have these transcripts because I'd have to know what these potential suspects talked about with the investigators, not their statements. The statements they have to give to me, of course, they have already provided some statements. But what these persons said in the interviews that preceded the statement because they were told that they were potential suspects, and according to the rules of the OTP they were duty-bound to videotape this, to submit a copy to this person, to have this person call a lawyer, and so on and so forth. So the Prosecutor is facing some problems that cannot be solved. The fact that the Office of the Prosecutor has a problem is something that suits me as an accused person, and they should deal with that without my help. Do not expect me to help the Prosecutor all the time as if it were in my interest to have the Prosecutor succeed in their intentions. No. My interest is to prove that they are incompetent, unable of handling this, and so on and so forth. All of this has to be on paper, all of it has to be in Serbian, and if you think that it is doable for me to listen to thousands of tapes for hundreds of days, that is impermissible. Nothing is known whether I am going to have some assistance or whatever, all of that has not been solved. And also how much can I give to such assistants. You know, so far, I gave assistants only material that I had read previously and then I would suggest to them the response should contain this, this, and that. Sometimes I'm satisfied, sometimes I'm not satisfied. Sometimes, I'm not satisfied with a motion that they prepare, and then I don't submit it. Also as far as experts are concerned, I give them the main points, what they should pay attention to and what is the thesis that they should try to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have to have a 20-minute break. Mrs. Dahl, you can have the floor again later, but the good thing about Mr. Seselj is every time he takes the floor it raises a new issue. This time we are talking about witnesses that were suspects and who were -- whose statements were filed, and we then had their statements. So Mr. Seselj is saying that these suspect witnesses have made statements, and I would like to have a recording or something from the interview before the statement or while the statement was taken. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Very briefly, I wanted to clarify the proposal regarding the provision of transcripts in B/C/S. Mr. Seselj will have all of them, he just won't have them before trial starts. He will have the transcripts relating to an individual witness at least a month before the witness appears, in B/C/S. He can have them today in he wants them in English, but he doesn't so we don't torment him by continuing to try to give them to him. That being said, with the suspect interviews, in ensuring that we have fully discharged our obligation, I want to also prepare transcripts in B/C/S of suspect interviews. Right now there are a couple that are available only in electronic digital format of the videotape that was created during the questioning. I will tender what I have to him because I believe it's his responsibility to decide whether or not to accept it; not mine to choose not to offer it to him. So if he rejects it, that's his choice, but it's incumbent on me to make the material available to him. If he doesn't like the format, that's a choice he has to live with the consequences. I will review the transcript to make sure if there's something more I need to add after the break that I take that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will now have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Let me greet the new OTP representative next to Ms. Dahl. You have the floor, Ms. Dahl, if you want to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think with regard to the suspect interviews, if we have any material that qualifies as witness statements and certainly somebody being interviewed with the rights of a suspect would have information regarding the commission of a crime, we will make sure that if that person appears as a witness his videotaped material will also be reduced to writing and in B/C/S. Sometimes those videotapes are complex to transcribe because you may have three languages going on at once, just as we do today. So we will make sure that the parts that need to be interpreted, are, and the parts that are already in the native language are simply transcribed. But those will be disclosed before the witness appears, but we are unable to complete transcribing all of the relevant material before the commencement of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj, Ms. Dahl has provided us with some positive information. She guarantees that when a witness comes to testify prior to their testimony you will have the translation into B/C/S of what that witness might have said in another trial. So that problem is settled. Secondly, with regard to the issue of suspects Ms. Dahl has just said that you are going to receive the translation of the interview of that suspect with investigators or sometimes there are English-speaking investigators, so the interview is in English but the suspect has an interpreter. Everything will be translated into B/C/S, however, so no problem there. Last thing -- yes, Ms. Dahl --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to clarify the difference between transcription and translation. If the witness has testified in B/C/S, there's an audio of his live testimony. We don't do anything other than transcribe that. If, for instance, an expert witness has testified, we will translate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the clarification. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, the microphone wasn't on. Judges, the problem has not been resolved. Mrs. Dahl said that if one of the suspects appears as a witness, then I will get the transcription of the interview with them, but I'm much more interested in the suspects who are not going to appear as witnesses and there have been many of those because that's potentially exculpatory material for me, it has to be made available to me. Everything that has to do with the process that is against me, the officials of the Serbian Radical Party, people linked to the Serbian Radical Party, volunteers, all that is interesting to me, and they have to deliver it. Then there are people who have been interviewed in the status as suspects, and in their fear they accepted to be Prosecution witnesses. However, when the mandate of the Tribunal was limited and that -- when it was said that the last indictments will be raised until 2007 or 2008, they gained some courage and refused. That is potential exculpatory material for me. If you want to give me all exculpatory material, then that includes all the interviews that the Prosecution interviewed as potential Prosecution witnesses and as suspects; without that material, I cannot defend myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are again raising two problems. There's the one about the suspects who are not in the 65 ter list, and you decided not to call them. Mr. Seselj is telling us that he wants to have the interviews because he's of the opinion, rightly or wrongly, I don't know, that the interviews might be exculpatory for him because it might be that the suspect sort of mitigated his guilt and so he wants to know about that and that's what he's asking for. The other category is that when you have continued with the investigation, you heard other witnesses who were not witnesses at the time of the indictment, but since the investigation continued and at the time the Prosecution must have asked them to be -- them to be Prosecution witnesses, which they turned down for some reason, and Mr. Seselj says that he wants to know those witnesses because they might prove to be witnesses that could sort of free him of his criminal liability. So what is your stand on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me take the points in reverse order, and I will tell you that I do not consider any witness to be a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness; these are Tribunal witnesses and they are called here by circumstance of history. I do not ask somebody's permission to call them, it is their civic duty if they are witnesses to a crime to bring the factual information that they possess that is relevant to the charges before the Tribunal. So it is a misstatement to say that there are a legion of former party members who have refused to be Prosecution witnesses or that we have battered into submission; that is simply Mr. Seselj's rhetorical flourish. The witnesses belong to the Tribunal and to their own events of history. With regard to suspect interviews conducted in the investigation, I will inquire of our investigative staff and my lawyers to see if there is someone other than those of whom I'm already aware, but I will not at this point jeopardize any witness's protected status by disclosing whether or not there are additional people that Mr. Seselj doesn't know about yet who may have fallen into a suspect/witness category. But I take very seriously the obligation to provide him with material he deems relevant and will exercise due diligence and make the appropriate inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I share your view. I too believe that they are witnesses of the truth of history, no problem there. But you did not quite answer the following problem. We had an indictment. Mr. Seselj had an initial appearance, he pleaded not guilty, and there was the status -- the pre-trial stage. And during the state, I suppose so, I don't know, but I suppose that the OTP carried on the investigation and asked various individuals to come, to be heard, and to give statements. So this Mr. X might have made a statement. After this, the OTP reads the statement and says, no, no, it's not relevant, no purpose to this, and it's not used by the OTP, therefore you sort of give up on that witness. If I understand Mr. Seselj - if I'm wrong he'll correct me on this - but he says that this type of witness is of interest to him. He wants to know what those people said to the OTP because it might be that they have exculpated me and so it might be a exculpatory statement, so under 68(i), I have to know about this, this must be disclosed to me. So this is what he says. And he wants to be apprised of these statements that have been recorded of witnesses that you do not plan to call but that you have on store in your archives, in your records. It may be wrong, it may not be the case, I don't know. This is quite a theoretical question, but he raises it. You may not know; I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's not theoretical at all. There's a prior Trial Chamber decision that directed the OTP to provide him with any witness statements mentioning his name, and we've gone to some length to make sure he's had all of that, including seeking disclosure of material that was otherwise protected by, for instance, a Rule 70 provider. So I believe that has been done, so if someone has mentioned his name in passing and replied with a negative: No, he's never been to Rome or, no, I never saw him there, he has that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me this hypothesis has already happened and you must have already disclosed the documents to Mr. Seselj already. There you go, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not true, Judges. A little bit of that material has been made available to me, but not the main part. They tried to disclose some of it in electronic form, which I did not accept. Since I have the floor, let me express my astonishment over the ignorance of the procedure in this court that Ms. Dahl is displaying. She says that all the witnesses appearing here are Tribunal witnesses, that is simply not true. That is so in civil law, but here in common law that is not true. What is the difference between Prosecution witnesses, Defence witnesses, and Court witnesses? I'll give you just one. With Prosecution witnesses, the Prosecution leads the examination-in-chief and I take the cross-examination. The process and the procedure is quite different. With Defence witnesses, it is the Prosecution that cross-examines. With Court witnesses, both the Defence and the Prosecution cross-examine in a way, and I have to take an educational role here. I have to edify her a little, there is a considerable difference here between Defence witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, and Court witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... taking note of this, you are right, too, but you know when a witness takes an oath, in doing so he becomes a witness of the Court, of justice. Mr. Seselj, with regard to the appearance of Mr. Oberschall, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not decide who is going to be the first Prosecution witness. I am prepared for the cross-examination of expert Oberschall, and in a few days I will submit to you my response to his supplemental expert report. And it is quite possible that you will soon receive the Defence expert report on the same issue by Mr. Dejan Mirovic, MA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now we come to the very purpose of this Pre-Trial Conference. We have another 50 minutes left. Under the Rules, the Trial Chamber is to determine the number of witnesses and the duration of the case. I'm reading this for the transcript, Rule 73 bis, Pre-Trial Conference, the Pre-Trial Conference is happening before the beginning of the trial. On the basis of the report made by the Pre-Trial Judge further to Rule 65 ter (L)(i), the Trial Chamber may call upon the Prosecution to shorten the estimated length of the examination for some witnesses. In the light of the files submitted to the Trial Chamber by the Pre-Trial Judge, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (L)(i), after having heard the Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber shall determine the number of witnesses to be called by the Prosecutor and the time available to the Prosecutor for presenting evidence. The Prosecution has provided us with a 65 ter list as well as with the estimated duration. On the basis of all this, the Trial Chamber takes into account that when we have the first witnesses, some time will be devoted to the Prosecution case or to the examinations in chief, and also to the Defence. Mr. Seselj will have the same amount of time for each witness as does the Prosecution, but you have to add on to that the questions by Judges. You must have understood already that I like asking questions, so I shall not refrain from asking questions and I'm sure that my fellow Judges will have questions themselves. And then every now and then we have procedural issues. Best is when we have very few of them because it's better to spend time on documents and witnesses rather than on quibbling on procedural matters, but it can happen. So the issue arising from all this is the estimated length of the Prosecution case. I'm repeating this. Trial Chamber I presided over by Judge Orie, when the trial started, had decided to set a time of 91 hours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 81 hours, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thereafter, there were new factors that came into play and 81 hours does not seem to be the correct figure. If I sum up the time estimated by the Prosecutor and if we believe the OTP, we should all in all have 170 hours, so just about twice as much as the amount decided upon by the Orie Trial Chamber. I looked into each and every witness and I listed the estimates from memory I seem to remember that there are insider witness, called insider witnesses, that's first category of witnesses; and then the so-called expert witnesses, for the time being ten of them are scheduled; then we have witnesses for various localities, Vocin, Vukovar, Petkovci, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Brcko, Bosanski Samac, Nevesinje, Mostar, and the Greater Sarajevo, and one last witness added on the 29th of March, and we do not have an information on that witness pursuant to Rule 65 ter. So all in all, we should have 101 witnesses. Ms. Dahl, apparently regarding Vukovar you have a lot of witnesses, and it might be that you could cut it down. Regarding municipalities, here too you could pare down significantly. So in sum, provisionally of course, the Trial Chamber will issue a written decision on this. We could think of 120 to 125 hours so that the Prosecution case may be completed around July or early September because of the summer recess. As to Mr. Seselj, he would start -- of course there can always be the Rule 98 bis, but I have to surmise here, so if there is no 98 bis application, he could start in September. And he would too have 120 hours, so September, October, November, January, February, so March, April, roughly that's the schedule. The Trial Chamber will seek the parties' opinions, but we have the case-law established by the Appeals Chamber. As to the determination of the length, the Trial Chamber has full discretionary powers of appreciation unless there is a discernible error by the Chamber. Recently the Appeals Chamber issued a decision in this respect, also when a length is set of course anything can happen. For instance, the Prosecution may decide to shorten. It can happen. Sometimes they are over-optimistic and they may not be able to call all the witnesses they planned to call, but there may also be situations in which the Prosecution may need extra time. Then they can apply to have an extension of time. Refer to what happened in the Milosevic case, the Prosecution had applied for extended time. So there's always flexibility. There is a decision of course that is issued by the Chamber, but it is a provisional one. The trial starts, and depending on the situations there can be changes. And what is good for the Prosecution is also good for the Defence because the two scales of justice are evenly balanced. Ms. Dahl, 120, 125 hours, what do you think?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, I'm very pleased to have the opportunity to begin the trial and we will look at the number of witnesses and the relevance of their testimony to determine how many we may not be able to call if it turns out that I can't persuade you to give me more time, but I think that beginning with the presumption of 120 to 125 hours is a good starting place, and I trust that if I can persuade you to give me more time because there's a good reason for it, that you'll exercise your discretion as you have the power to do; and if we need less time, then of course we'll contract the case accordingly. One concern that springs to mind is with regard to the municipalities. We have made the case as skinny as we can. My worry is that when so much rides on the credibility of one witness, because we're asking so much of them, to represent what's happened to their entire community, that we don't risk proving too little by relying on one person for so much. So I will keep in mind the comments regarding the depth of the evidence, but we're dealing with massacres of families and mass graves with hundreds of people. And I don't want at the end of the day to be short-changing the victims or the international community by presenting what I hope is a compelling and persuasive case, only to have it rest on the shoulders of one or two sturdy survivors. But I'm grateful for that duration of the case and we will be as efficient as we can and try to bring you the very relevant pieces of evidence and not more than you need and not less than you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj, you also have your word to say because you are indirectly involved, even if we're talking about Prosecution witnesses right now, you are entitled to cross-examination. So you're also entitled to the same length of time. So this would mean for the time being that the Prosecution would be given 120 or 25 hours for their expert witnesses, for the insider witnesses, or the municipality witnesses. As for you, you two would have 120 hours. I want to say this but I know you know because you taught me last time, you plan to testify in person, and further to the Rules and the case-law of the Appeals Chamber, the time taken by an accused when he testifies is part of the total amount of time given to the Defence; in other words, if you need 40 or 50 hours to testify, if you have 120 in all, you have to deduct the 50 hours. So you have 70 hours for the other witnesses. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that is clear to me. I will have a very small number of witnesses in addition to the experts and myself, who is going to testify both in chief and in cross. There will be witnesses who will be examined in chief for only 15, 20 minutes. I'm not going to stretch things like the Prosecution are doing. However, I have to raise four issues, or rather, ask four questions. Some things are not clear to me. At the Status Conference I remember the figure of 105 witnesses was mentioned, now it's 101 apparently. Which four witnesses were left out? Second, how is it possible to question in the Prosecution case that number of witnesses in 125 hours, if we bear in mind that some will take five or six hours? The Prosecution announced lengths of eight hours for some witnesses. It doesn't sound possible to me. Now, the problem arises, how is it possible to lead evidence on the pattern of conduct in the municipalities that were left out of the indictment when the indictment was reduced about the purpose and methods of joint criminal enterprise without crime-base evidence. If we have no crime-base evidence on Vocin, Brcko, Konjic, Borasnica, and other places, if there are no -- if there is no crime-base evidence in these localities, then there is no evidence of the pattern of conduct because the two or linked. The Prosecution apparently plans to lead crime-base evidence although that was denied them by a decision that you confirmed this year, a decision dated in last year. I believe this Trial Chamber has to deal with this problem urgently. The indictment was reduced by five locations, five localities, but the number of witnesses and the number of exhibits has not been reduced; that is unclear to me too. Next, the trial is beginning tomorrow and my objection to the indictment has not been resolved yet. I have submitted it within the deadlines set by the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, I believe your decision on protective measures is untenable. I invoke Rule 65 -- sorry, Rule 69. Rule 69 says the protective measures may be applied in extraordinary circumstances and that the identity of a victim or witness must be disclosed in sufficient time prior to the trial to allow adequate time for the preparation of the Defence. So in sufficient time prior to the trial. Despite your interpretation that the beginning of the trial is marked by the first Prosecution witness, the beginning of the trial is actually tomorrow. The beginning of the trial is actually the opening statement by the Prosecution. And generally speaking, the Rules of Procedure do not leave the possibility of disclosing material on a witness 30 days prior to that witness's appearance. There are six such witnesses according to your decision. I believe your decision has to be adjusted to the Rules if you really want a fair trial. Those protective measures may be justified of course, but disclosure of the identity of protected witnesses may not be stretched that long. If that identity is revealed to me 30 days prior to their appearance, those 30 days for me will be taken up by preparing for cross-examining other witnesses. It is too little time to prepare to cross-examine a protected witness. All these names must be revealed to me in sufficient time prior. There are quite a few witnesses in respect of whom you have decided that their identities will be known to me only 30 days before the -- their appearance and some witnesses I will know only 30 days before the beginning of the trial. In addition to these, their identity -- there are witnesses whose identities I should know, although they remain protected. The number of those identities that have been revealed to me is negligible with respect to the total number of witnesses, and that kind of disables my Defence. So if we deduct these 16 witnesses, because I am operating with a figure of 105 from the latest Status Conference, out of the remaining 89 I don't know even half of the names. If you believe that based on these facts you are able to conclude that all the pre-trial requirements had been satisfied, then the trial will commence tomorrow. But these objections of mine remain. I will continue to repeat them tirelessly throughout the trial and in the appeals proceedings, because they have a firm standing in the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You have asked four questions. Some pertain to what Mrs. Dahl has said. I shall answer those that relate to the Trial Chamber. If my colleagues wish to intervene, they may. As you know, protection of witnesses is provided for in Rule 75 and 69 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It so happens that in your file a lot of witnesses have already testified in other cases. That seems obvious. In the other trials these witnesses benefitted from protective measures; therefore, we don't have any room to manoeuvre. The Prosecution has filed motions, the Trial Chamber has handed out decisions. Believe me, everything has been scrutinised on a case-by-case basis. And this Trial Chamber, but the other Trial Chambers as well, and prior to this one have handed down such decisions. So there will be witnesses whose identity you will know 30 days before the trial, and in some cases, some witnesses you will get to know 30 days before they come to testify in court. This is something we discussed last time. We discussed what would happen before the commencement of trial. As you know, I have handed down a decision that we had to wait for the beginning of the trial before we could have the first witness. Because let us imagine that on the 11th of December, for whatever reason, you fall ill and you cannot come. If, in that case, we would have set tomorrow's date, we could no longer apply the 30-day rule. This is why after having given careful thought to it this time-limit 30 days before the trial begins is the 30 days before the trial -- the witness comes to testify. Because tomorrow we will hear the Prosecution, after tomorrow we will hear you, and we could have started with the first witness on Monday. That wouldn't have been a problem whatsoever. It so happens that given the number of trials ongoing and courtrooms that are not available and the fact that the Judges are otherwise busy, we cannot hear this witness before the 11th of December. But whatever the case may be, without it prejudicing you in any way, you will have 30 days before the 11th of December, i.e., the 11th of November, in few days' time. You will have the list of those witnesses mentioned in the decisions, i.e., 30 days before commencement of trial. As far as the other witnesses are concerned, those that will benefit from additional measures 30 days before they come to testify, well, that will depend on the Prosecutor. I know nothing about that. Perhaps the Prosecution will call those witnesses sooner or later, I don't know. Mrs. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the topic makes me think it's a ripe moment to address this request to the Chamber. I received the Scheduling Order setting the commencement of evidence for the 11th of December. That contracts the time from six days we expected in December to three, and I'd like to request a modification of the decision of 16 October concerning protective measures for certain witnesses. The reason for this is that after we finish the week of 11 December, we will then go into a three-week winter recess. The effect of that recess coming so quickly on the abbreviated schedule for December is to dramatically diminish the protection for witnesses, and I think that there is a demonstrated need for protection and would like to propose that we disclose our witnesses who have the benefit of the protective measure of delayed disclosure on the 11th of December. That affords the accused the 30 days before we get back into this trial schedule that will resume in January and does not cut in half essentially the protections for those witnesses. It's an unfortunate combination of events that we have a very brief sitting followed by a very lengthy recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution is making a new application which I discover at the same time as you. Let me sum it up, the Prosecution has realised that we will be sitting on the 11th, 12th, and 13th of December, and then we have a three-week break, which means that if the disclosure is made on the 11th of December, we will run into difficulties because we will have the three-week winter recess which will come into play then. So the Prosecution is suggesting that the Trial Chamber states that -- we're not talking about Mr. Oberschall in this case because he's not concerned, but this would start running from the week in January when we will start hearing the witnesses. I think if I'm not mistaken that should be around the 7th or the 8th of January, I don't have a calendar in front of me, which means those 30 days would apply as of the 7th or 8th December and not as of the 11th of November. It's a little bit complicated, but as I know that you have an agile mind, I would like to ask you whether you wish to respond to this orally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, at law schools in my country - and I hope that that is the case throughout the world - during the freshman year there is this subject called general theory of law and state. Within this subject there is a long section that has to do with the interpretation of law, and there are different methods there. When I took that exam - and I was an excellent student - had I interpreted legal norms in that way, as is happening in this courtroom, I never would have gotten a degree in law. In all textbooks at law school it says that a trial starts with an opening statement of the Prosecutor or in some case -- in some countries the indictment is read out. For example, in Serbia, in the beginning it is the indictment that is read out. Nowhere in the world does a trial start from the day when the first Prosecution witness is heard. That doesn't exist anywhere. Secondly, no matter what you decide now, you are going to stand by them. It has to do with your own reputation as a Trial Chamber. Rule 69 does not allow for that interpretation. In 69(C) there is only a reference to early enough prior to the beginning of trial, nothing else. It doesn't say 30 days prior to the testimony of a particular witness. That cannot be legally valid. Perhaps it can take place through legal violence, but then your previous decision has to be questioned. It is going to constitute legal violence. You cannot trample upon Rule 69. It is explicit. It says in sufficient time prior to the trial, let it be one day, let it be one hour before the trial starts. If the trial starts tomorrow at 9.00, I insist that at 8.00 in the morning I get the names of all protected witnesses, otherwise you are committing legal violence. Make it happen at 8.30, make it happen at a minute to 9.00, give me a list of the names of protected witnesses and I am going to admit to you that that is early enough prior to the commencement of trial. But interpreting it to say that the trial begins in December and in view of the fact that Oberschall will only be heard for three days and then the next witness comes in January, and then we consider the first day of the trial in January to be the beginning of the trial, that's a comedy. From the first moment this trial is being turned into a comedy. I insist that a minute before trial starts I be given a list with the names of all protected witness, otherwise this is legal violence. In the morning before Ms. Dahl starts her opening statement of the Prosecution, if I do not have a list with all the names of all the protected witnesses, you will be directly trampling on Rule 69 and this is legal violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you know the Rules of Procedure, and you quoted Rule 69, quite rightly so. If you will allow me, I shall read paragraph (C). "Subject to Rule 75, the identity of the victim or witness shall be disclosed in sufficient time prior to the trial to allow adequate time for the preparation of the Defence." So on the 11th of February, 1994, those people that have drafted this provision were careful to make sure that the Defence was in no way prejudiced. I assume that it's on the basis of this paragraph (C) that the case-law was established by the Trial Chambers here, and this is why the time provided for someone to prepare his or her Defence is 30 days by and large. Therefore, with this in mind, what should guide the Bench is the question of whether the accused has enough time to prepare his Defence; otherwise of course this does infringe your rights. 30 days is something which was worked out by all the Trial Chambers. It's not mentioned in Article 69 -- in Rule 69. For those witnesses which you will discover 30 days before, let me remind you that you've been preparing this case for the last five years. And more than anyone, I'm sure you know all the witnesses and potential witnesses that may come to testify from back to front. So you should be able to cross-examine these people. So the Trial Chamber has noted what you have said. You challenge the application made by Mrs. Dahl. The Bench will discuss it, and I cannot tell you outright how the Trial Chamber will respond. But we have acknowledged your submission. You have also raised another issue. You said that at the outset there were 105 witnesses and that there are only 101 now. I -- this is a figure I quoted on looking at a document. You are the only person who knows how many witnesses you plan to call. Mr. Seselj is able to do his sums, and he thought 101 witnesses, some of them will be here for four to five hours, maybe you'll run into difficulties. So how can we hear 101 witnesses in 120 hours. So could you perhaps clarify this for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I don't think that I can. I think that the premise of the question is difficult if all of the witnesses take each four hours or so, of course we can't bring everyone we would like to with the time we've allotted. Our estimates are based on an abbreviated presentation in court. Some witnesses may do no more than adopt -- swear to the 92 ter statement that they have prepared. Other witnesses we will lead more evidence from orally, depending on their prominence and proximity to the acts and conduct of the accused. Some witnesses we will bring in with their statements and simply tender them for cross, trusting that the information contained in writing will be deemed relevant and compelling as if the witness had read his heart to you, so to speak, from the witness stand as opposed to simply putting his signature at the bottom of his narrative of events in history. If we are unable to proceed by way of written testimony, written form, like a dossier of evidence that a witness has affirmed and sworn is the truth, the time allotted to us will cripple the Prosecution case. I don't think that is the intention of the Chamber, certainly the goal is a fair and compelling presentation of evidence that's relevant to the charges. So we will try to efficiently use the court time, giving more to witnesses for whom the cross-examination may be more robust and less to those witnesses where we would hope that the material facts are not contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are addressing the issue of witnesses, I would like to mention, this is for my colleagues and this was mentioned in my report. Mr. Seselj filed a few months ago a complaint for contempt of court re: Number of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, including the person heading -- the chief Prosecutor. So the Trial Chamber was presided over initially by myself and Judge Robinson and Judge Bonomy. We had handed out a decision and stated that these witnesses who had been pressured or tampered with in any way, during the cross-examination of Mr. Seselj, that these witnesses could be questioned, and the questions could pertain to promises, forms of pressure exerted, and so on and so forth, which means that in light of this decision which was handed down, Mr. Seselj, when a witness comes to testify - I'm not talking about Mr. Oberschall in this case, but I'm talking about other witnesses - and the Prosecution will conduct its examination-in-chief and will say, Can you confirm or stand by the written statement you have made, let me show you the document. And once this is done, then you will have time -- you will still have time, and this is mentioned in the 65 ter rule. And if the Prosecution has to ask, you will then have to ask to cross-examine, and we are complying with the decision that was handed down by the Trial Chamber. In other words, to put questions to the witness relating to the fact, understanding how things happened with the OTP, with the investigators, were they given promises, were they given gifts, why in the end did these people come and testify. So any question pertaining to the credibility of the witness are questions you will be entitled to put. I myself will put questions to those witnesses in light of the question you have raised. The Trial Chamber at the time was presided over at the time by Judge Robinson and the Trial Chamber has said -- had said that it was only after hearing all of the testimonies that the Trial Chamber would look into the merits of your complaint. And you will be able to bring in your own witnesses in support of your allegations. Therefore, I wish to remind you of this. This has not been forgotten, and I personally will put questions to the witness to this effect and check those conditions or under which conditions these statements were made. So tomorrow the Prosecutor, Mrs. Dahl, I believe it's you unless it is Mrs. Carla del Ponte who will come and honour us with her presence, I don't think so, but I think it is Mrs. Dahl who according to the Rules will provide us with her opening statement. She will give us the position of the OTP in this case. So this is what we will hear tomorrow. I would like both parties to make reasonable statements. And, Mr. Seselj, even if you don't approve or agree with what Mrs. Dahl is saying, please do not intervene. The same applies to you, if you are saying something which displeases Mrs. Dahl, please let him finish. Last time we did say that the Prosecution would have four hours. And, Mr. Seselj, you will have the same amount of time, four hours also. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit, Judge, that I'm surprised by your words of caution. Not at a single conference did I interrupt Ms. Dahl. Tomorrow I'm going to keep totally silent. I really do not think that you should have warned me about this. If anybody is prone to interruptions, it's Ms. Dahl. I never ever interrupted anyone. Secondly, you invoked 69(C) in the sense of it guiding us to Rule 75. That is true. But Rule 75 does not offer the possibility of disclosing the names of witnesses to an accused 30 days prior to their testimony. Rule 69 is categorical. If it was violated in some cases, that had to do with Judges' arbitrariness, and I don't think that you should rely on that in this case. I demand an absolute honouring of Rule 69, and I insist that you inform me in the morning before Ms. Dahl starts with her opening statement what you decided as a Trial Chamber on this particular matter, whether the names of protected witnesses have to be disclosed to me before the trial starts or through some kind of an absurd interpretation of who knows when. The other thing that Ms. Dahl said that many witnesses would be 92 ter witnesses and 92 quater, again I would like to call upon Rule 6 that prohibits that, the retroactive change of provisions of the Rule that would prejudice my rights or jeopardize my rights, and that would certainly be the case because I was not present when these witnesses were interviewed, when their statements were taken. I did not have an opportunity of questioning them. Their alleged statements are only an extension of the indictment for me. This is not evidence. If that is evidence, then you can take the indictment as evidence, too. If you look at a statement that was written by the Prosecutor or an investigator and if you're taking that as evidence, then you can take the pre-trial brief as evidence, then you can take the indictment as evidence, and there is nothing more to be done. I do not accept a single witness on the basis of Rule 92 ter and 92 quater. It is only through legal violence that that kind of thing can be admitted into evidence. You cannot convince me that this is not to my detriment; it is always prejudicial against me and I'm not going to cross-examine witnesses like that. You did not answer another question of mine: What about my motion to -- in respect of objecting to the indictment. I'm actually referring to Rule 72 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... respond straight away. The motion on a defect in the form of the indictment is something which we are looking into. I wanted this current Chamber to hand down this decision, not the previous Chamber. So this will be done. As far as what you've just said concerning 92 ter, 92 quater witnesses, we've already had this discussion at the last Status Conference and I did tell you that according to Rule 6 the amendments in force or the amendments will come into effect the day they are published without it prejudicing in any way the rights of the accused. Therefore, what is going to happen? When Mrs. Dahl will say, I would like a 92 quater because my motion meets the requirements of a 92 quater rule, when the Trial Chamber will hand down its decision it would consider whether or not you are being prejudiced. If you are being prejudiced, then you can say so because you will also be entitled to speak up and you will tell us what the prejudice concerns. Now, as far as 92 ter is concerned, if a witness is heard as a 92 ter witness, he then takes a solemn declaration and testifies under oath and he says that he is going to tell the whole truth, namely, that what is contained in the statement is in line with what he will say, then you can and you are entitled to cross-examine him on everything that is contained in his written statement. That is how 92 ter rule operates. This is what I told you last time. However, this will have to be decided on a case-by-case basis. I don't know what kind of witnesses will be called. If in any event one witness is called to testify and that that witness may pertain to your responsibility, then maybe the Bench will turn around and say, No, no 92 ter, please, because it is important for that witness to answer the questions that are being put to him or her by the Prosecution. And in that case, a written statement will not be taken into account. But this will be decided on a case-by-case basis. As the Trial Chamber will know ahead of time which witness will come when and how, then the Trial Chamber of course will be able to, after having heard you of course, because it is very important that we hear what you have to say in these proceedings and if your rights are being infringed and if you are being prejudiced in any way, the Trial Chamber will then say yes or no. So your rights are being guaranteed. The Bench is going to discuss this in a few minutes' time. As you have filed a request and told us that you would wish to have the list of witnesses by tomorrow, and pursuant to Rule 69, we will tell you what the Bench has decided. But I cannot anticipate the decision of the Trial Chamber regarding this particular matter. This is what I had to say to both parties. This 73 bis rule hearing is coming to a close, and pursuant to this rule we will hand down a written decision on allocation of time. And before giving the floor to Mrs. Dahl tomorrow morning, we shall hand down an oral decision on this particular matter; namely, the witnesses which you would like to be informed about. I would like to thank both parties, the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, and I would like to thank the parties for the way in which this hearing has unfolded. We were able and you were able to express yourself freely. I hope this will be the case in the future. This is in the interests of justice, and it is important to have an adversarial debate here. It is important that each party states his or her position so that the Judges when it comes to deliberating are able to determine the matter on the basis of the relevance and probative value of the evidence. This is what should help us on this difficult exercise which is what we are asked to do here, i.e., to render justice. We have to make sure that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence are abided by, that both parties are protected in these proceedings, and that the accused has a feeling that the trial has been fair. If it were to be to the contrary, justice would not prevail as it should. I am sure that my colleagues also share the same view as I do.
